items.title: Man jailed for grooming at least 70 girls online
paragraphs: A man who groomed at least 70 girls and manipulated them into sending sexually explicit videos and images of themselves has been sentenced to 30 years in prison.
Bilal Kazi, 27, targeted his victims - aged between 10 and 17 - using apps including Snapchat, Wink and Roblox between August 2021 and August 2025.
Kazi, a student from India who was studying at the University of Chester, posed as a 14-year-old white British teenage boy and made his victims believe they were in a relationship with him.
He was jailed after pleading guilty to 37 charges including making indecent images, blackmail and inciting a child to engage in sexual activity.
Warning: This article contains distressing information
Kazi must serve a minimum of 20 years in prison before being eligible for parole and will be on the sex offenders register for life.
Once eligible for parole he will be on licence for eight years.

In a personal impact statement read out at Chester Crown Court earlier, one victim said she had struggled with anxiety as Kazi, who later moved to Birmingham, had "taken away a sense of privacy and security".
"I am doing my best to move forward but the effects are still with me," she said.
"The harm caused is not limited to the time events took place - they continue to affect my daily life."
The court heard that some of the victims had attempted suicide, struggled with anxiety and developed eating disorders.
One victim, who was 13 years old when Kazi first contacted her, said he took her "innocence away".
"I hope one day I can get on with my life," she said.
Judge Stephen Everett said Kazi was a sexual predator who took advantage of "what appears to be a lack of proper security on social media sites".
"It is incomprehensible to me why any person would do what you did to those little girls," the court heard.
"This was bad enough, but when one learns of all the other images you demanded for your deviant sexual desires, we will never know how many victims there were.
"Children who believed they were safe in their own homes - and by your gross misuse of social media - you took away all of that safety, all of that comfort."
The judge said it was difficult to find any mitigating factors and said he doubted Kazi's remorse.
"You are a very dangerous person," he said.
"In a sophisticated way, you got into the minds of young people and got them to do things that were totally alien to them."
Talking about one victim, Everett said: "She won't look back on her childhood with any great pleasure - she will look on it totally blighted at what this fiend did to her."
He added: "These are not just pictures on a computer these are young lives that have been blighted."
Det Con Georgia Hughes, from Cheshire Police, said Kazi had not shown any remorse.
"The girls targeted by Kazi were young and vulnerable," she said.
"For many, their interactions with him were their first experience of what they believed to be a romantic relationship.
"Exploiting that trust, Kazi manipulated them into believing that his behaviour was normal.
"Many lived in constant fear of what he would do if they failed to comply with his demands, and some have carried that fear with them for years.
"What should have been important formative years have instead been overshadowed by the trauma of Kazi's abuse."
Speaking on online safety, Sgt Ross Peel said the force's message to parents was to "speak to your children and take an interest in the apps and platforms they are using".
"The potential for online offending is vast," he said.
"And offenders can target children from anywhere in the world.
"By educating yourselves and your children about online safety and the risks associated with communicating with people they do not know online, you can help protect them."

items.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
paragraphs: Election workers process vote-by-mail ballots at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on Nov. 5. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption

In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene.

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.
Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a press conference Thursday. Win McNamee/Getty Images hide caption
But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.

"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."
Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.

One key ruling, which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government could appeal.

In an earlier order in October, a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."

Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.
"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."
What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.

In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."
President Trump added on Truth Social: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.

In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.

The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.
The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.

Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."
Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.

"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."
Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.

Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.

The federal government has never maintained a complete list of U.S. citizens. Trump administration efforts to cobble together citizenship data from various sources have led to naturalized citizens being mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, and data experts have warned the federal government's methodology in California was likely to also lead to false matches.

The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge allowed data experts from University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project to analyze the DOJ's list of 20,000 names. The analysis found 42% did not appear on California's current voter roll and that naturalized citizens were on the list.
Separately, several California counties have noted the lists from DOJ were riddled with duplicates and obvious inaccuracies.

Santa Cruz County's top election official, Tricia Webber, wrote in an email that of the 81 people DOJ had listed as suspected noncitizens registered to vote in her county, "more than half are not registered in Santa Cruz County; some names do not match any person currently registered or previously registered," and some dates of birth "were wildly inaccurate with some dates appearing well into the future like 2044."
Even DOJ attorneys acknowledged in court hearings under questioning from judges that there have been flaws with federal lists of likely noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton nominee, who was presiding over the federal government's lawsuit against California, had planned to hold proceedings that would assess the accuracy of DOJ's lists. That will no longer happen since the DOJ dropped its lawsuit.

For Loyola Law School's Levitt, questions remain about whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter roll data for this project without following required public notice procedures.

And with Democrats winning control of Congress, lawmakers could hold hearings that probe deeper into how federal officials came up with their list, said David Becker, the executive director for the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"I think we're going to have some very serious scrutiny of the Department of Homeland Security and their methodology as they assisted the administration in its failed effort to try to demonstrate there was widespread noncitizen voting in this country," Becker said.

items.title: The new Apple TV has a YouTube problem
paragraphs: A software update and a reboot should get YouTube working on your new Apple TV 4K.
A software update and a reboot should get YouTube working on your new Apple TV 4K.
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

People who received the brand new Apple TV 4k today saw some strange error messages as soon as they opened the YouTube app. As the first units arrived, the app was initially only showing a black screen with a QR code and an error message saying “YouTube is not yet available on this device.” In some cases the app was functional, but had a transparent red bar stuck at the bottom of the screen saying, “YouTube app is approved for device testing only and not for production use.”
Installing the new tvOS 27.2 update and rebooting wasn’t enough to resolve the issue for The Verge’s Tom Warren, he also had to uninstall and reinstall the app.
The Verge’s John Higgins said in his review of the new Apple TV 4K that it’s “one of the best streaming devices available,” but expensive compared to other streaming boxes.

items.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
paragraphs: The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".
It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".
When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".
"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.
Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.
"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."
Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.
Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.
One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.
He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.
The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.
The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.
Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.
"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."
He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

items.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
paragraphs: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.

And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

items.title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
paragraphs: The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.

“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.

The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”

Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”

In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”

Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”

Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”

Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

items.title: These IEMs get the Most Beautiful Earphones Award for 2026, but will their crowd-pleasing tuning win you over?
paragraphs: The ZiiGaat Seraphim IEMs stand out from the crowd because they just look so god damn beautiful. Luckily, their beauty's more than skin deep, and fans of rumbly sub-bass and an airy treble that brings detail to music without tiring your poor ears out will rejoice. But I can't help noticing that lean lower midrange which can take away some of the fullness of music that other IEMs at this price point keep.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I read recently that the Chi-fi space releases 200+ IEMs each year. It definitely feels like it, though when you disregard the crap and focus in on quality brands like ZiiGaat, Dunu, Kiwi Ears, Aful and Juzear, it's a far more manageable 100!

Price: $259 Release date: October 20265 drivers: 2DD + 3BAMaterial: CNC-machined aluminium shells, faceplates, and nozzlesCable: 1.2m modular (3.5mm & 4.4mm)Impedance: 9Ω @ 1kHzSensitivity: 125.5dB/Vrms @ 1kHzWeight: 5g each

Amongst the wave of IEMs to come out in 2026, I don't think I've been more excited about the look of an IEM than with the ZiiGaat Seraphim. And the more I found out about these beauties, the more excited I got about their sound.

Tuned by the consistently excellent Jay Audio, and combining two dynamic and three Knowles balanced armature drivers, the Seraphim promises a flagship-tier listening experience without – at $259 – the accompanying destruction to your wallet.

At this price point, they're not going to make my list of the best budget IEMs under $100, but there's every chance that they make my buying guide to the best IEMs under $500. Read on and see if they sound like the right option for you.

Overall sound: There was online chat about the Seraphim being a mini-Storm, but that's actually a bit of a red herring. I heard the Subtonic Storm at CanJam London, and from memory, it has much less emphasis on bass, noticeably fuller mids, and a significantly more nuanced, airy treble presentation overall. Instead, the Seraphim offers an exciting, contrasty sound with strong bass and a well-balanced treble. The mids are a little lean for me, and won't be for everyone, but if you're looking for sub-bass impact, these are your boyees!

Bass: The Seraphim uses an isobaric dual dynamic driver configuration that is meant to be good at delivering deep frequencies. I have no way of testing whether that's true, but what I can tell you is the sub-bass hits like a truck. In a good way.

Rather than bleeding into the lower midrange, the mid-bass remains tightly controlled, prioritising accuracy over bloated warmth. I really like this, as it provides a sense of bounce and grip texture, where bass guitar lines from Dry Cleaning's MySoul / Half Pint feel satisfying, while electronic kicks and 808s sound authoritative, separated, and just a blast to listen to.
However, this separation of upper bass and lower mids, while eliminating bleed, brings its own issues to the tuning...

For all my headphone and IEM reviews I play them through my Luxsin X8 and Chord Mojo 2 desktop DAC/Amps, as well as several dongles. This ensures sufficient power for peak performance, and provides a transparent source for a clean, detailed signal. My music sources are Spotify Lossless and CDs.

Midrange: Again, if marketing materials are to be believed (they're not, they're not!!) the Seraphim's Knowles balanced armatures allow the midrange to lean toward a clean, analytical profile that slightly favours upper registers.

For me, the midrange has pros and cons. Higher register vocals, such as Neil Young on Tell Me Why, are forward and engaging, cutting through the arrangement with transparency. But the lower mids feel a tad lean, stripping some natural body and chest resonance from vocals, especially on the lower tones of Barry White on Can't Get Enough of Your Love.

Despite this minor honkiness on certain vocal tracks, the instrument separation is really good, making every piano plonk and acoustic guitar strum sharply defined. I think the upper mids are so balanced that overall the timbre of the Seraphim is good, and instruments sound 'right', on the whole (though this is definitely where the Seraphim falls down against the CrinEar Reference – see the comparison section below for more on that).

Treble: The treble response is probably the most impressive part of the Seraphim's tuning. It delivers a highly resolving, crisp presentation without harsh peaks. It just seems to be very well balanced, offering a well-extended presentation, with just enough air to bring sparkle but without the tiring glare that you often get with bright IEMs.

I hear plenty of micro-details and coupled with the massive sub-bass, you could call this a very exciting V-shape tuning. Now, there's no perfect tuning, and especially when it comes to treble, one person's subtle spotlight is another's midday sun aimed at your eyeballs, and I think the Seraphim's treble can get a little much. But that's only on music that's mixed bright, like Michael Jackson's Billie Jean or Lucinda Williams's Sweet Old World.
But on 80% of my music library, the treble is smooth and fatigue-free, allowing for long listening sessions.
Price: At $259, the Seraphim sits in a competitive mid-fi price zone where consumers rightfully expect premium technicalities, durable accessories, and engaging tunings without glaring flaws.

And you get all of that with the Seraphim! It offers good detail retrieval, a thunderous sub-bass response, modular cable terminations, and a quality metal build that justifies its relatively modest asking price.
But how does it compare to the competition?

This is slightly unfair, as the Seraphim isn't going for the same style of tuning as the neutral Reference. Yet it's worth comparing, because at $350 the CrinEar Reference offers what I would describe as a far more sophisticated sound. There are lots of fun, exciting, contrasty, V-shaped IEMs out there, like the Seraphim. At the time of writing, there's only really one truly exceptional neutral IEM: The Reference.

When placing the Seraphim alongside the Reference, it's impossible to ignore the visual similarities. Aesthetically, the Seraphim is definitely trying to steal Crin’s lunch, mimicking the sleek metallic faceplates and minimalist shell contours. And Jay does it better! The Seraphim looks so much more engaging and visually interesting than the Reference's bland logo faceplate.

As mentioned, the sound is totally different. Where Crinacle goes for strict neutrality, emphasising natural vocal timbre and a smooth yet full midrange, the Seraphim leans heavily into a more flash, fun, V-shaped profile. It aggressively pushes that thunderous ten-decibel sub-bass slam and analytical treble, trading tonal purity for excitement and flair. And sometimes that's what I want! Most of the time, I get plenty excited by the balanced brilliance of the Reference.
Another area the Reference wins in is comfort. For me, the longer, deeper fit means a better seal is achieved quicker than with the Seraphim.

Pitting the Seraphim against the Binary EP321 is more of a fair fight. First of all, at $310 the Binary EP321 is more comparable price-wise. It's also a visually interesting IEM with its multi-coloured, reflective faceplate.

Sound-wise, it's a bright IEM with enough sub-bass and mid-bass to justify the 'exciting' descriptor. I think it does mid-bass better than the Seraphim, and with its extra treble, there's more detail in that bass with the EP321.

Most important for me, the EP321 is less lean in the lower mids, injecting much-needed warmth and thicker vocals that the Seraphim can lack. As mentioned, the Binary EP321 provides more treble energy thanks to its MEMS driver (says the marketing), meaning ultra-high frequencies are achieved with blinding speed.

Ultimately, if you crave physical sub-bass impact, grab the Seraphim, but if you prioritise airy treble and natural lower mids, the EP321 wins out easily. For me, I'd always go for the EP321 over the Seraphim.

ZiiGaat has fully embraced sturdy metal shells, providing an understated faceplate design that feels solid without being heavy. Although I've read online that some people don't like the thin cable, I'm a fan of it! After all, when was it decided that thick = great quality?! It wraps easily and avoids annoying microphonics entirely, which are major plusses for me.

In terms of ergonomics, the robust nozzles create a rather noticeably shallow fit, so I couldn't use my favourite Juzear eartips, as I wasn't able to get a proper seal, and instead I used the new rounder tips that came with the Dunu Vitruvian IEMs, which are longer. I still had issues with achieving a seal when swapping them with other IEMs for comparisons, but I don't expect many people will be doing that, and once I got the seal, it stayed, so I don't want to overstate it.

The Seraphim is mid-sized and I find them very comfortable when fitted. This makes them a good choice for long daily commutes or extended listening sessions at your desk without any noticeable fatigue.

I'm confident that the ZiiGaat Seraphim will be many people's idea of perfect in an IEM. Their tuning is ideal for audiophiles wanting visceral sub-bass impact combined with pristine detail retrieval. EDM fans and gamers will get on with them, with its punchy dynamics and superior imaging. They also look stand-out-beautiful, and though that's not enough by itself, it's a hell of a big plus in my book. After all, my favourite IEM is the CrinEar Reference, but I far prefer the look of the Seraphim!

Listeners seeking lush, thick male vocals should look elsewhere, as the lean lower mids will prove frustrating. However, despite a few subjective quirks, it remains an incredibly competent hybrid monitor, and I really liked it for the vast majority of my music library.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?
paragraphs: You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Fox has officially acquired Roku and there are CONSEQUENCES. For one, the "Marine Aquarium" screensaver will no longer be available. One person posted on the "Mildly Infuriating" subreddit: "I can't believe it I love my fish what am I gunna do."

The artist behind that screensaver, Jim Sachs, is NOT renewing his license due to Fox's acquisition. "It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can't stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole," Sachs told Ars Technica. The licensing deal will have big personal consequences for Sachs, who relies on the $80,000 per year licensing deal. Another comment on the subreddit posted, "This is the last straw, Apple TV for me."

What to Know: Over the past decade, European countries have become increasingly reliant on U.S. technology to support their air defense systems. We're talking fighter jets & missile defense systems like the Patriot, which can intercept ballistic missiles. It seemed like an obvious choice: these are high-quality pieces of technology, they're readily available, and buying American keeps the U.S. committed to European defense. Here's the problem: the whole "readily available" thing doesn't seem to be true. There is a MAJOR backlog of missiles while demand just keeps going up. That's due to both production delays and the U.S.' own military needs in Iran. PLUS!! European countries that bought technology like the Patriot are now locked in to American equipment. They can't just switch to another supplier to get missiles.

Visitors queue to take a closer look at a Patriot missile launcher during the Armed Forces Day at the Airbase in Laage, Germany, on June 06, 2026. Along with nine other locations, Laage hosts the Armed Forces Day 2026. JOHN MACDOUGALL/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption

Why this matters: You kind of want to know if you're not gonna get a few hundred missiles on time. While the U.S. is focused on the Iran war, threats from Russia still loom large in Europe. And now, many European nations are at the whim of these defense contracts panning out… having to put up with delays and higher costs. The article's authors look back and see a missed opportunity in 2022 for investment into homegrown systems: "Calls to Europeanise the funding and ordering of air defense systems were ignored and the strategic gap is now all too visible."

Business journalist and friend of the show Paddy Hirsch adds: "No one could have predicted the extent to which Trump would damage the relationship between the U.S. and Europe. But the fact is that Trump isn't the first president to beat the drum about European over-dependence on the US. He's just the first to really force the issue. And guess what? He was doing Europe a favor! Europe desperately needs to wean itself off the U.S. teat, and not just because of the unpredictability of a Presidential whim. But because there's no telling how U.S. and European interests will diverge over the next few decades."

What to Know: Spain has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. It's currently at 1.1, meaning 100 women birth 110 children on average. To maintain the current population, rates would need to sit at 2.1. Immigration has kept the population from dropping dramatically since 2000, but the author offers a DIFFERENT solution to Spain's childbearing woes: more housing. Spain, like many countries, has struggled with expensive housing: prices have risen 81% between 2015 to 2025. The average age of leaving the parental home in Spain is 30.2 compared to 23.8 in France and 24.1 in Germany. The author asks: could an influx of public housing incentivize partners to start families earlier?

How realistic is this?: There's no hard evidence in the Elcano article showing more housing actually leads to a higher fertility rate. That said, Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo says the evidence for this argument does look stronger outside the U.S. There was literally a paper about this topic IN SPAIN that came out a few weeks ago. The paper found a 10% rise in local housing prices LOWERS birth rates by about 3% for women 20-34. In fact, the authors deduced that higher housing prices account for roughly HALF of the 2014-2022 implied fertility rate decline. In short: more expensive housing = fewer kids.

If you HAVEN'T listened: We all know the old adage "the stock market doesn't equal the economy." Well, lately, maybe it does!! At least more than usual. The "new era" economy (AI, tech etc.) has an outsized impact on the growth of both the stock market AND economic growth. That's all well and good, except hyper-concentration means hyper-risk. If AI stocks start to tumble, it could have a negative chain reaction on the economy in a uniquely problematic way. Two non-profits in the episode warn that the AI bubble is a thing. In short, the economy depends on the market! A downturn there is more likely to mean an economic downturn too. Diversification is important, people.

If you HAVE listened: You know that the economic risk isn't just about a market downturn. It's about the impacts that follow. Consumer spending is driving much of economic growth, and that's led by wealthy spenders. Another downstream risk: pension funds hold debt related to the AI buildout, according to the report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. They argue this has exposed pension funds and even ordinary workers to dangerous risk! Reporter Wailin Wong says, "That's something I wasn't able to get into in the episode, since we were focused on stocks and not debt. But certainly the credit markets are a huge part of this story too."
Reporter Ricky Mulvey read A Violent Masterpiece
It's a profane, no-holds-barred thriller. Jordan Harper wrote on TV shows in Hollywood before getting disillusioned with the industry and writing about some of its seedier parts in novels.
A Violent Masterpiece follows three storylines that converge around a suspicious death in a jail cell. It's Eyes Wide Shut meets LA Confidential.
Two things I really admire about Harper's work.

A Violent Masterpiece is a perfect book to rip through on a plane if you are traveling for the holidays. A genteel reader should stay far away, and sickos should pick it up. The story is far from perfect; you'll see why at the ending. I loved it.

items.title: UK-EU deal will ‘dissolve’ £60m a year of costs for plant trade, says Angela Eagle
paragraphs: The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said.

Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November, Angela Eagle said she hoped paperwork headaches for importers would “disappear” after the changes, although the move would not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls.

“If we get the ink dry on 20 November, which I very much hope we will … all of that uncertainty, the extra cost, the paperwork and the potential problems if things get stuck at borders would all disappear,” Eagle told the Guardian during a visit to a plant nursery in Kent.
“The cost, that £60m, can just dissolve and people’s potential to both export back into the EU and get their imports in … gets easier and more predictable.”
The UK’s departure from the bloc triggered the introduction of border checks on imports and exports of plants, food and animal products, from sausages and cheese to trees and leather goods.

Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit, according to analysis by the National Farmers’ Union, with egg, chicken and potato producers badly affected.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed between the two sides in May, is due to be signed at next week’s summit. It will permit the removal of the vast majority of physical checks and most of the accompanying certificates and paperwork.

This will save businesses in the horticulture sector the current cost of trading with Europe, including plant health inspection fees, phytosanitary certificates, document and ID checks, port fees, agents’ fees, additional labour costs and extra haulage costs.

These costs total £60m a year, according to calculations by the industry body the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), but do not include late delivery penalties or sales lost because of port delays or damage to goods.
These savings should put “downward pressure on food prices”, Eagle said, although she would not confirm the deal would lower the cost of food in the UK.

The promise of the deal was welcomed by Provender Nurseries, one of the UK’s largest wholesale nurseries, which sells thousands of plants, trees and shrubs to local authorities, parks and landscapers from its base at Swanley in Kent.
However, the company has already spent at least £500,000 on building a post-Brexit control post on its eight-hectare (20-acre) site, which will become obsolete once the deal is implemented.

Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, said the business constructed the “sealed building and bought four electric forklifts to operate in it” to allow inspections of lorry loads of valuable trees and shrubs imported from the continent.
The company decided to build the site to reduce the “delays and damage” it had experienced when smaller loads were inspected at government-run border control posts such as Sevington.
“It cost a lot for a barn, but it gave us security as a business,” said McKenna.

Despite this, McKenna hopes the SPS deal will convince some of Provender’s European suppliers, previously deterred by the paperwork and potential pitfalls of post-Brexit trade with the UK, to restart exports.
“We need to see the small print on the agreement,” he said. “It could have been sooner, but we are pleased that it is happening.”
The deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028, meaning businesses such as Provender will still be subject to the current border arrangements for more than a year.

In the meantime, Fran Barnes, the chief executive of the HTA, called for “some easements as a transition arrangement that are pragmatic” to help horticulture businesses, such as fewer or no checks on imports of lower-risk products.
Eagle conceded the implementation date was later than the mid-2027 targeted when the former prime minister Keir Starmer announced his EU “reset” deal in May 2025.
Starmer’s replacement by Andy Burnham led to a “pause” in negotiations with Brussels, said Eagle, with the upcoming November summit pushed back from July.

The original target was “always a very, very ambitious timescale,” she said. “That extra time has meant we could deal in a more coherent way with some of the knottier, thornier issues on things like pesticides.”
The UK has continued to use some pesticides and fungicides that are banned in the EU.

This has prompted industry concerns that British potatoes grown in 2027, treated with pesticides banned in the EU, could need to be thrown away if the resulting frozen chips went on sale after the deal’s implementation.
“We are very well aware of these kinds of issues and the EU is also very aware it doesn’t want to be seen to be wasting food,” Eagle said.
British exporters of produce including seed potatoes and some mussels also hope the SPS deal will allow trade halted by Brexit to restart.

“We have been waiting for this moment, but it all depends on the timing of the deal,” said Adam Taylor, a director of Taylors Bulbs in Lincolnshire, which supplies tulip, daffodil and other bulbs to garden centres and nurseries across the UK and Ireland.

A Brexit certification disagreement halted exports of British seed potatoes, particularly from Scotland, to the EU. Taylors underwent the “laborious and expensive” work of setting up an Irish business in order to keep supplying the Republic of Ireland.
“When things go back closer to how they were before Brexit, I hope our Irish customer base will reflect on the loyalty given to them,” he said.

items.title: The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
paragraphs: Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.

We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.

Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.

Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.

For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.

Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.

Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.

Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.

WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.

Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.

If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.

Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.

Smart TVs are often pretty dumb. If your dad is always complaining about his TV, or if you want to get ahead of it, grab the latest Apple TV 4K. Although it’s not cheap, it stands out with built-in mics for Siri AI, lots of power, HomePod surround sound support, and a simple, ad-free interface.

The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.

Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.

The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.

BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.

The Rival Pro offers plenty of thoughtful extras, including swappable batteries and an ultra-wideband base station for a seamless, low-latency connection. The gaming mouse’s lightweight design and 8,000Hz polling rate also deliver both accurate and ergonomic performance for up to 16 hours per charge.

It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.

Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.

For the manga or live-action Netflix show lover on your list, this fashionable Pirates jersey, inspired by Monkey D. Luffy from the seminal pirate adventure series One Piece, will be as surprising as it is delightful.

If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.

Zero Company, a strategy game set in the twilight of the Clone Wars, is a fun way to get lost in the Star Wars universe. The single-player, turn-based title lets players command a diverse team of characters across a gorgeous expanse of worlds, offering hours of solitary entertainment.

If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.

We fell for Apple’s handy iPhone strap due to its effortless accessibility and comfy design, which uses flexible magnets to keep excess segments in check. From biking to hiking to concerts, it’s a great way to sling your iPhone 18 Pro, assuming you have a compatible phone case.

The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.

Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.

This battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in job. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. It can be controlled from an app and even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet, powerful, and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.

Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.

If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.

Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.

The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.

When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like a pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.

Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.

items.title: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
paragraphs: Senator Chris Van Hollen speaks at a rally outside of the U.S. Capitol in support of USAID — the United States Agency for International Aid — on February 5, 2025. The Maryland Democrat has just announced that he will challenge Senator Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Nathan Posner/Anadolu/via Getty Images hide caption

"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.

As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?
Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.

There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.
One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.

We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.
We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.
You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?
Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.

One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.

One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.

There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.
The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?

When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.

The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.

So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.
What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?

This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.
Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.

If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?

I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.

I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

items.title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
paragraphs: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.
But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.
The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.
For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.
In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.
This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.

That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.
Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.

They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.
The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."
In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.
German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.
The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.
And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".
The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.
"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."

However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

items.title: Adobe's Black Friday deal is its biggest in years, with 57% off Creative Cloud Pro
paragraphs: The Adobe Black Friday sale has begun, and it was worth the wait if you've been holding out to lock in a year of savings on the world's most popular creative software. From today, you can save 57% on an annual Creative Cloud Pro subscription (new users only).

That includes Photoshop for digital art and image editing, Lightroom for photo editing, Premiere for video and Illustrator for vector art and graphic design. It's still the industry-standard package for professional creatives, and if you're in the US.

The Adobe Black Friday discount extends to the students and teachers plan, which is reduced by 77% to $15.99 for the first year. Pricing in other regions varies but often with similar discounts. Here are the details. In the UK, the price is reduced from £66.49 to £28.49 per month.

While there's a lot of competition in creative software today (see our guides to the best graphic design software and the best digital art software), we think Adobe's Creative Cloud still has the edge.

It's convenient to have a complete ecosystem of apps that integrate into multitool workflows, especially now that an increasing number of artists and designers are working across various media, from 2D design to motion graphics and video. Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq.
