items.title: First Ferrari Style flagship in New York features metallic facade
paragraphs: Architecture studios Formafantasma and Gonzalez Haase AAS have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in New York, clad in a metallic facade.
Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.
Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

Under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.
“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.
The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.
However, the New York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” said the team.
“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”
Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.
The space is bordered by a deep red curtain and large rectangular ceiling lights.
A staircase to the left side of the store leads to the “more intimate” second level, containing women’s ready-to-wear, footwear and accessories collections.
It also contains the store’s atelier, the second worldwide apart from the London location.
Wrapped in leather curtains, the space provides a private setting for personalisations and alterations. A table containing samples of textiles and hardware sits at the centre.
Ferrari Style, the brand’s luxury fashion line founded in 2021, has other US locations in New Jersey, Miami, and Las Vegas.
Ferrari recently unveiled a laptop collaboration with HP, as well as its first electric vehicle earlier this year.

items.title: Microsoft outage live: millions still affected as disruption stretches beyond 18 hours
paragraphs: Readers in the US may be surprised to wake up to the news that Microsoft's outage is not fixed!

While North America was asleep, there has been widepread disruption around the world – from schools, courts and public services in Australia, to companies and government services in Japan, and then schools, the police and the NHS in the UK.
The cause of the mega-outage, which began around 18 hours ago, is still not known.
Microsoft says it has “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident” at this time.
Reminder, it reported around 45 minutes ago that the situation was improving in Europe, Japan and North America.
Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example:
Problems with Exchange Online mean users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web
Microsoft 365 Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.
Microsoft Copilot 365 – users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps
The Microsoft To Do app may not load, and users may see operation failures.

double quotation markMost of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats.

Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.
Microsoft: We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability
US jail unable to release prisoners due to Microsoft outage
Tampa: emails disrupted, full restoration expected within 48 hours
Microsoft: continuing to see improvements
MS: 'broader improvements' in North America
Microsoft reports 'encouraging' progress in recovery in Europe
NHS England: Staff are turning to paper records
Schools inspector Ofsted, and universities, hit by outage
Railway passengers may have problems with emailed tickets
Bank of England caught up in Outlook outage
UK healthcare system seeing 'widespread' and 'serious' disruption
Microsoft: We're seeing 'early signs of stabilization'
Tell us: have you been affected by the Microsoft outage?
NHS organisations reports issues with Outlook and Teams
UK government putting 'contingency plans' in place
UK police can't receive crime reports online due to Microsoft problems
UK government engineers 'working with Microsoft' now
Microsoft outage has "major impact" in Japan
Microsoft: we're seeing positive results for server stability
Microsoft: seeing 'marginal success' patching servers
Tech giants and international airlines say they’ve been hit by outage
Microsoft’s global outage will cost Australia billions, expert says
Microsoft outage may persist as fix is 'not taking as expected'
Victorian government warns of opportunistic scammers amid outage
'Looks like we will have to talk to people’: Australians on their email-free day
WA government: 'Microsoft are prioritising life, safety and Government services'
What we know so far about the global Microsoft outage
Microsoft having issues bringing servers back online
Microsoft ‘do not believe they are dealing with a cyber event’, Tony Burke says
Schools, courts and public service staff affected
Thousands of Australians report issues with Microsoft 365
Microsoft may not be able to deliver your email, but it has a fine knack for writing up incremental progress towards fixing its outage.

double quotation markCurrent Status: We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability as recovery progresses across affected Microsoft 365 services. While service functionality continues to improve, some users may still experience intermittent connectivity issues or delayed email delivery.
This is one of the longest and most disruptive outages Microsoft 365 has ever suffered, reports Professor James Ferryman, professor of computer science at the University of Reading.
Professor Ferryman explains why it’s taking so long to fix:

double quotation markThe problem is in Exchange Online, which is the email and calendar system behind Outlook. Teams and Copilot rely on it too, for calendars, meetings and getting at people’s work data. So when Exchange has a bad day, a lot of other things do as well.

“What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering. The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. You can’t just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit.
Astonishingly, the Microsoft outage is preventing some US prison inmates from being released!

The Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office in Colorado, USA, has warned they cannot process bond payments, as they rely on Outlook email notifications. So unless the money is handed over in person, people can’t be let out.

double quotation markThe Microsoft outage is affecting online bond payments for individuals being held at the Arapahoe County Detention Facility. Because of the outage, jail officials are not receiving the email notifications needed to process online bond payments.

Until Outlook email is restored, anyone needing to post bond for immediate release must do so in person at the jail. We apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate your patience. For questions or additional information, please call 720-874-3500.
Shares in Microsoft have dipped slightly at the start of trading in New York
They’re down 1.1% at $516.86 – a fairly modest reaction to bringing down a decent chunk of the world’s email services.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at trading firm XTB , says:

double quotation mark“This is the third Microsoft outage in a year, and raises questions about whether Microsoft can service its AI enhanced products. The market does not appear overly worried about the situation…
If services are not back up and running in a quick and smooth fashion, then the sell off could get worse.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Chair of the UK’s Science and Technology Committee, has commented on the Microsoft Outlook outages:

double quotation mark“The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services.

“My committee’s report on delivering a digital government concluded that the UK is hugely dependent on a small number of US-based technology providers for our public services, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing. In its response, the government could not tell us how much it was spending on IT and digital or who it was spending it with - without even knowing this, how can we protect against vendor lock-in or achieve the resilience and digital sovereignty the UK needs.”
Microsoft has suffered a certain amount of snark due to its continued service outage.
Britain’s Royal Mail posted a photo on X of one of its trademark red post boxes with a simple message: “No Inbox, No Problem.”
The message at the top of the post said: “Ours is always open.”

However, Royal Mail’s track record for service delivery is not beyond criticism either! One X user has proposed adding a community note, flagging that MPs predicted it will deliver 219 million letters late this year….
Now it’s the turn of American towns and cities to warn residents that services are affected by the global Microsoft service outage.
The City of Tampa, in Florida, has warned it is “currently impacted”
And it warns it could take up to 48 hours to restore services fully:
City of Tampa offices are open and operating on normal schedules. Walk-in services, phone lines, and emergency operations (911) remain fully operational.

However, residents and external partners may experience delays or failures when sending emails to City of Tampa accounts or receiving emails from them. Technology teams are actively monitoring the Microsoft issue and based on vendor guidance, full service restoration is anticipated within 48 hours.
The Microsoft outage may be an – unwelcome – opportunity to test how companies and public services would cope under a serious cyber attack.
Forrester’s principal analyst Dario Maisto epxlains:

double quotation mark“The Microsoft outage, for the little we know so far, represents the perfect quasi-natural experiment for stress testing an organization’s - and even an entire continent - digital sovereignty posture.

“Although this outage does not strictly pose a sovereignty question, as this seems to be more an accident than the consequence of a government’s will, it does allow us to test what would happen if interruption of mailing services and AI tools like Copilot would be the direct consequence of a political act from the government.
Microsoft has now declared that service availability continues to improve – but dome users may still have problems accessing their email.
In an updated Current Status on the outage, it says:

double quotation markWe’re continuing to see improvements in service availability, with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels. Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as recovery continues.
Simon Azzopardi, CEO of security firm CoreView, says IT teams need to do three things following the Microsoft outage:
double quotation mark“Confirm that security and compliance controls such as data loss prevention, sensitivity labelling and Intune compliance policies are working as intended.
Review every emergency change made during the outage, because workarounds made under pressure tend to become permanent gaps.
And treat delayed email with extra caution: Microsoft warned that Safe Links might not be able to check URLs during the disruption, and attackers routinely use outages as cover.”

double quotation mark“Our sympathy goes out to every IT team that has spent their time keeping their organisation running without email, calendars and, in many cases, their security and compliance tools.”

items.title: Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to block Megaspeed
paragraphs: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, of failing to properly oversee the export of high-specification Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.
Jensen Huang left the company he co-founded after revelations he had an affair a former Megaspeed executive. The firm had been buying advanced chips from Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling those chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
Bessent also said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.

"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.

items.title: Europe should not walk into Russia’s ‘traps’ on Ukraine talks, EU’s foreign policy chief Kallas says – Europe live
paragraphs: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned against the EU agreeing to Russia’s proposed sequence of talks on Ukraine, saying it would allow Moscow to “divert the attention away” from its actions and ultimately leave Europe “in a worse place.”
She welcomed the US side “finally admitting what I said already one and a half years ago – that for any deal between Russia and Ukraine … you also need the Europeans.”
“I hope that we are just not at the table, but we are actually also really influencing the outcome of these negotiations.”

“The most important is that we keep to our agreement that first the ceasefire, then peace agreement and then any kind of other talks … when Russia is still presenting their maximum demands, then we should also stick to the maximum demands and start to negotiate from there. …

Kallas warned that there is a risk of Europeans “actually walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as Moscow is trying to “divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire and actually [get us to] start to listen to their claims.”
“If we walk into that trap that we start to discuss … the European security architecture, then I don’t think we are in a better place. We are actually in worse place.”

“Let’s focus on what it is at hand. We have one aggressor and one victim. The aggressor does not have security concerns, as nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
Kallas is also very clear that she wants to be part of the EU negotiating team, saying she was appointed to represent Europe on foreign and security policy.
“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say on who is representing Russia? No, we don’t.”
She also said that ultimately she would not be “representing myself,” but bound by any mandate given to her by the 27.
Slightly amused/frustrated with repeated questions on what’s holding up the EU with deciding on its representation, she eventually hits back with this line:
“Well, we have institutions in place, so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending. Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”
Asked why she thinks the Russians do not want her to be involved in the negotiations, she says:

“They don’t want [anyone] strong on the other side because they want to push their through their maximum demands, like they have always done. Because … their tactics is very clear: at first you present threats and ultimatums, you use force, and then you will just wait, because there will always be people in the west who will offer you something you didn’t have before. And every time you go further.
So, of course, if you negotiate with anybody, you want the other side to be as weak as possible so that you can get what you want.”
Reported Russian demands on Ukraine, Europe have no chance of succeeding - snap analysis
Europe needs to show it can 'contribute' before being allowed to join Ukraine talks, Russia says
'Please, no surprises,' Merz urges Trump ahead of his meeting with Putin in China
German drone maker supplying Ukraine reports cyberattack
Denmark's Frederiksen urges more help for Ukraine to help it get through 'tough, tough' winter

EU leaders meet in Dublin to talk Ukraine, AI
Meanwhile, German tabloid Bild has reported on what it says are the key Russian demands put forward in negotiations with Europe, Ukraine, the US.
It includes a number of maximalist demands which would dramatically alter the security landscape for Ukraine and Europe.

We already knew about some of them – for example, Russia’s demand to keep the occupied Ukrainian territories and the entire Donbas region, demilitarise Ukrainian ports and keep Ukraine out of Nato – but there are also some new ones, including a reported request that Nato should not have any bases in the Baltics and that Finland, which only joined in 2023, should be made to leave the alliance.

The list also includes new proposals on Moldova, which Moscow reportedly wants to turn into a federal republic and then force referendums on the future of two of its regions, Transnistria and Gaugazia.

If this list is true – which we do not know that and have not been able to independently verify it – it is probably fair to say that it’s just not going to work and will only anger Europeans at the time when the US wants to get them formally involved in the process.
Ukraine has been repeatedly clear that it has no intention of giving away the temporarily occupied territories, and even less of signing off the parts that are actually still controlled by Kyiv.
And Finland’s defence minister Antti Häkkänen also made it clear that the demand on Finland’s Nato membership has no chance of succeeding.

“These matters are not up for negotiation. Russia knows that and it’s absolutely outrageous to even suggest this,” he said, quoted by Finnish public broadcaster yle. “Finland will not be forced out [of Nato],” he added.

The chairman of the Finnish parliament’s foreign affairs committee, Johannes Koskinen, told reporters that “if such a paper or demand has been submitted, it will go straight into the bin,” IS reported.
Lithuanian foreign minister Kęstutis Budrys also made it clear earlier this week that Lithuania would block any agreement giving Russia the power to stop Nato deployments in the region.

While there’s a lot of foreign policy discussion happening in Dublin, another key issue is the race in artificial intelligence, with EU leaders trying to strike a balance between not falling behind against the US and China while also trying to protect citizens from some of the associated risks.
Roberta Metsola, president of the European parliament, said she was tired of hearing that the EU had “somehow lost the AI race”.
“We have world class talent, we have a great... ecosystem from a technology perspective,” the president of the European Parliament told reporters before the summit began.
It’s worth noting that while Anthropic and OpenAI often dominate headlines, Europe has its own frontier lab, Mistral, which focused on delivering an open-weight model.
For her part, foreign policy chief Kallas warned about a “dark side of AI”, citing the example of how its being used in warfare.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin said that Europe must show it is ready to contribute to the Ukraine peace ⁠process before a decision ⁠is made on letting Europeans join ​the negotiations.

The comment by Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov suggests Russia has not yet committed to including Europeans in the next round of talks, despite US negotiators saying on Thursday that president Vladimir Putin ⁠had agreed to their participation, Reuters said.
Asked if peace talks would soon resume with the added participation of Europeans, Peskov said:

“Once we ​understand their genuine intention and readiness to contribute to the peace process, ‌then it will be possible to ‌make a decision on holding dialogue on a Ukrainian settlement in an expanded format.“
“If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorised in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them.”

Speaking in Dublin, German chancellor ⁠Friedrich Merz pleaded ⁠for US president ​Donald Trump to create no surprises ⁠during expected talks about Ukraine ⁠next week with Russian ​president ‌Vladimir Putin ‌in China.
“Some here ‌in Dublin fear this could turn into a ‘second Anchorage moment’,” said Merz ‌on the sidelines of a meeting ​of EU leaders, as reported by Reuters.
“I therefore want to state our message ⁠to the United ​States very ​clearly: please, ​no surprises. Continue ​to ‌play ​as ​part of ’Team Europe’ and ’Team Ukraine’”.
Merz also said that Europe does not need to discuss the European security architecture with Russia, a new Russian demand in any peace process on Ukraine.

“Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists,” Merz said, adding it was a “given” his country would be part of any European delegation, AFP reported.

Meanwhile, German defence group Quantum Systems faced a cyberattack last month that prompted the German military to briefly ground its fleet of the company’s drones, with suspicion falling on Russia, sources told AFP.
Attackers are increasingly targeting European defence firms supplying Ukraine for its fight against Russia.
Quantum, a producer of reconnaissance drones and other unmanned systems based near Munich, said “hostile actors” launched the cyberattack in late October.
“The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities,” it said in a statement.
There was no risk to operations of the firm’s systems, it said. The company declined to give further details.

Fun aside, the host camera captured an interesting exchange between Ireland and Denmark’s Frederiksen, with the Danish PM stressing to the Irish leader the importance of agreeing on a winter support package for Ukraine.
She said more help was needed to “get them through a tough, tough winter.”
“So if everybody could put something on the table, that would be very welcome,” she said.
Some other fun nuggets from the doorstep (10:53) include Croatia’s Andrej Plenković joking that Ireland’s Martin “is always here” rooted in the same spot where he welcomes the leaders.
Meanwhile, Poland’s Donald Tusk got a cheerful “dzień dobry” – good morning in Polish – from the official leading him through the building.
And if you’re wondering what the leaders are talking about between themselves on the doorstep, then I’m afraid the answer is very boring: it’s mostly the weather.
Several other leaders also remarked on how beautiful Dublin looks in the morning sun, with their arrival handler joking: “it’s always like that in Dublin in November… almost.”
The only two who had any, let’s say, doubts about the weather were, unsurprisingly, two southern leaders: Cyprus’s Nikos Christodoulides and Greece’s Kyriakos Mitsotakis.

In contrast, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Finland’s Petteri Orpo, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Austria’s Christian Stocker even opted for a nice stroll to the venue together.

This caused a bit of a diplomatic protocol challenge in terms of who should go through the door to see Ireland’s Micheál Martin first, with everyone stuck in an awkward cycle of pointing and “oh, please” until Merz eventually suggested Frederiksen go first, suggesting “ladies first.”
“Lady first,” she said, with a bit of a side eye, and stepped ahead.

Apparently, last night’s dinner at the National Gallery, prepared by Mark Moriarty, was also “excellent,” I am sure you would want to know – so much so that France’s Emmanuel Macron went to see the chef to praise him.
The food included smoked wild salmon from Cork, Wicklow-reared beef, cabbage grown in Dublin, and rapeseed oil produced in Donegal, RTÉ reported.
Either way, the doors to the meeting room are now closed, and the discussions under way.
Meanwhile, Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs has a strong entry for the quote of the day competition, as he said “we, as Europe, have to grow some bigger balls.”
“I think we as Europe have to grow some bigger balls, because we are bigger in size, … in military might, in all the economic aspects.
Look where is Russia: Russia is not capable of even taking such an, in size, in population, smaller power as Ukraine, which is showing a great, great spirit and fighting back [for the] fifth year.

And Russia is [now] raising points that we have no accept? Sorry, that’s the aggressor, losing on the frontline. We should be raising our expectations, what has to be done in terms of Ukraine’s security.”
Hungary’s Péter Magyar is also here, looking very elegant as always…
… but it looks like he took a slight detour on the way back to hotel last night to try and pour a perfect pint of Guinness.
Luxembourg’s PM Luc Frieden is in a slightly unusual position this morning as he is representing as many as three countries at today’s meeting in Dublin.
Belgian and Dutch PMs have skipped the summit as they face political problems at home, leaving Frieden with three hats and representing not his usual 690,000 people, but some 30 million people today.

“We had a meeting of the Benelux prime ministers two days ago in Maastricht. And so I know that when I speak here on their behalf, that on the fundamental issues that are being discussed here today – Ukraine, AI – we are very much aligned.”
He says he has got “some of their speaking points” from Belgium and the Netherlands to help him get through the meeting today.
He stressed that the three Benelux countries “are on the side of Ukraine,” and that “there is need for solidarity of all 27 member states” on further financial support for Kyiv.
On who should represent the EU in any future talks, he said “we cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” and suggested EU’s Costa “has an important role to play.”

There’s also a bit of national news on the side, with Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson confirming he will send his proposal to the Swedish Centre party later today in the latest bid to break the deadlock and form a new government, more than 60 days after the election.

The party – which could decide the shape of the next government – has asked the leaders of the centre-left Social Democrats and centre-right Moderates to share their proposals on how they could work together in office.
The deadline expires this afternoon, and hopefully the exercise will get us a bit closer to resolving the current standoff.

Both offers have their problems: the more natural, centre-left grouping, led by S’s Magdalena Andersson, is paralysed by the Left’s demand for cabinet decisions – a move the Centre party has said would be unacceptable.

But the alternative, led by Kristersson, would equally pose awkward questions for the Centre Party vis a vis the far-right Sweden Democrats – although the party offered they could remain in opposition, but support a minority centre-right government.
Kristersson sought to strike a conciliatory tone in Dublin, as he courted the centrists:

“I recognise that the Centre Party is under immense pressure right now – at times, the rhetoric has been quite harsh, bordering on insulting. I have no intention of engaging in that; instead, I respect the Centre Party’s right to choose its own path.”
“I do not intend to go into the details of the proposals we are presenting to the Centre Party; these are intended for their own internal deliberations.
However, I can say that this is a policy reform agenda representing a centrist, center-right political approach.”

On Ukraine, Kristersson said “what Russia does speaks volumes more than anything Russia might say during various negotiations,” saying he does not have “high hopes” about the current talks – but they still were worth pursuing.
He said the discussion on who should represent Europe is “slightly overstated,” as the focus should be on Europe’s interests, not personalities.
He said that some of the issues are “pure EU interests” to be represented by EU institutions, but others should involve the largest countries, including also the UK.
“I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

“The most important is that we keep to our agreement that first the ceasefire, then peace agreement and then any kind of other talks … when Russia is still presenting their maximum demands, then we should also stick to the maximum demands and start to negotiate from there. …

Kallas warned that there is a risk of Europeans “actually walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as Moscow is trying to “divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire and actually [get us to] start to listen to their claims.”
“If we walk into that trap that we start to discuss … the European security architecture, then I don’t think we are in a better place. We are actually in worse place.”

“Let’s focus on what it is at hand. We have one aggressor and one victim. The aggressor does not have security concerns, as nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
Kallas is also very clear that she wants to be part of the EU negotiating team, saying she was appointed to represent Europe on foreign and security policy.
“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say on who is representing Russia? No, we don’t.”
She also said that ultimately she would not be “representing myself,” but bound by any mandate given to her by the 27.
Slightly amused/frustrated with repeated questions on what’s holding up the EU with deciding on its representation, she eventually hits back with this line:
“Well, we have institutions in place, so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending. Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”
Asked why she thinks the Russians do not want her to be involved in the negotiations, she says:

“They don’t want [anyone] strong on the other side because they want to push their through their maximum demands, like they have always done. Because … their tactics is very clear: at first you present threats and ultimatums, you use force, and then you will just wait, because there will always be people in the west who will offer you something you didn’t have before. And every time you go further.
So, of course, if you negotiate with anybody, you want the other side to be as weak as possible so that you can get what you want.”

It’s a pretty chilly morning in Dublin, but the European Council president, António Costa, is keen to signal to his hosts that he’s ready to do business, showing off a cute Irish green scarf to Ireland’s Micheál Martin.
Today’s host, Ireland’s Micheál Martin, said discussions will focus on what Europe needs to consider any future Ukraine settlement a just and sustainable peace.

“The substance of any peace agreement is as important as who represents Europe. Europe needs to be very clear in terms of what would constitute a sustainable peace for the continent, well into the future. Security guarantees are a significant part of that, and also the reconstruction of Ukraine.”
He said the outstanding questions on Europe’s priorities and representation need to be decided “in the next week or two.”
On AI, he said the meeting will “explore the implications of AI, positive … plus the potential negatives, and the balance between regulation and innovation.”

Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has warned that Ukraine faces “winter … like hell again,” with Russia “bombing everything” as he urged European leaders to double down on their backing for Kyiv.
“Putin has to change his goals because the war, aggression, and killing of women, children, and civilians would stop right now if he gave an order.”
“The European plan for a while [has been] quite simple: help Ukraine push Russia and so should it be.”
Michal warned that Putin’s attempt to discuss the broader European security architecture before agreeing to end the war is “a mental trap” by Russia’s Putin.
“Does anybody really think that Europe is a threat to Russia? This is not sane talk to be honest.
So, I would say that our red line is quite clear: we should have peace, on Ukraine’s terms, and after that everything can be talked, but not before and not at the same time.”
The Estonian PM also said that if the EU needs to send its negotiators, the European Council president António Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are “the persons to do it”.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen insisted it is “self-explanatory” that Europe should be included in the peace talks on Ukraine “to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine.”
“We will come forward as a commission with a proposal for the financing of the Ukrainian needs in 2027, and with the 22nd sanctions package before the next European Council,” she said.
von der Leyen also said today’s talks would focus on “the risks … but also the opportunities’ associated with the rise of AI.
EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine today, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged them to “pay attention” to Vladimir Putin’s demands on security.
European leaders meeting in Dublin on Thursday rejected calls that there was any need to recreate a European security architecture, while restating that Russia needed to stop attacking Ukraine.
European Council president António Costa summed it up:
“There is no need to reinvent the wheel. Europe had a functioning European security architecture until it was first, gradually undermined, and ultimately destroyed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”
Speaking to reporters the UK prime minister Andy Burnham said Europe “in the wider sense” i.e not just the EU, would decide on its own arrangements.

“In terms of the wider point, there was a very strong feeling that you know, Russian demands to put the question of European security architecture or European security arrangements into this negotiation – that is not up for negotiation... It is for Europe to decide its own arrangements. Europe and Europe alone. And again, I am talking in the wider sense when I say that.”

Around 40 countries, most of the attendees of the European Political Community summit on Thursday, signed a declaration drafted by France declaring that European states “bear a primary responsibility and are assuming greater responsibility for the security of Europe”.

EU leaders are continuing talks in Dublin on Friday, focusing on AI. But following interventions from Giorgia Meloni and Friedrich Merz, they will also discuss Europe’s role in international peace talks and the question of future financial support for Ukraine.
EU leaders are meeting in Dublin today for discussions on Ukraine and AI, among others, as they continue their search for a lead EU negotiator in any peace talks with Russia.

Their discussions are becoming increasingly urgent, after Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, US envoy Jared Kushner said last night after meeting Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin.
“This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X.
But, as he somewhat mockingly said on Wednesday,
“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.”
Let’s see what comes out of these discussions, with the leaders also expected to talk about AI.
Elsewhere, I am still keeping an eye on the Dutch government crisis as Rob Jetten works hard to avoid the collapse of his minority cabinet.
It’s Friday, 13 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

items.title: Climate action discussed at youth COP meeting
paragraphs: School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.

The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.

Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues."
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."

items.title: 'Hardest challenge of my life' - Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need ride
paragraphs: Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.
The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.
The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised £3,853,530 in the process.
Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%.
"I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."
The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.
He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.
Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.
"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."
Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.
During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.
It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.
The broadcaster also expressed his gratitude for the support of Radio 2 listeners.

His messages of support from public figures included one from the Princess of Wales, who recorded a message for him in Welsh, saying: "Hi Owain, it's Catherine, you're doing so well. Keep going. Wishing you all the very best."
Shania Twain was so impressed that the bike had been named after her that she sent a message of good luck before the challenge.
She said: "Hi Owain, Shania Twain here. You're about to take on an incredible challenge for BBC Children in Need, cycling 400 miles through all four nations.
"As you set off in Glasgow, I just want to say: 'Let's Go, Owain!' We'll be cheering you on all the way. Good luck."
She sent him another message when he finished, saying: "Congratulations on completing your incredible challenge for Children in Need. You're still the one my friend, sending you all my love."
Helen Thomas, head of Radio 2, said: "Owain truly captured the hearts of the nation this week as he battled through his epic four nations Challenge.
"On behalf of all the Radio 2 listeners as well as the thousands of children and families who will benefit from his Herculean fundraising efforts we simply can't thank him enough. Diolch Owain! "

items.title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
paragraphs: A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.
The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.
There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.
In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.
Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.
Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.
Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.
He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.
"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"

Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.
He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".
Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."

Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.
Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."
Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.
As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."
Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".
McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."
While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.
Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels.

Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.
Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.
Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".

He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

items.title: Kisses galore, seaside shenigans, McRoman adventures and street feats – the week in art
paragraphs: Nicole Eisenman A free display beside the seaside from the witty and imaginative sort-of-figurative artist. Turner Contemporary, Margate, from 14 November to 11 April
The Last Human Kiss Snogging galore by Wolfgang Tillmans, Tracey Emin and other contemporary romantics. Sainsbury Centre, Norwich, until 11 April

Roman Scotland Images of classical gods, tombs of fallen legionaries and mysterious relics of Pictish life in a journey to the edge of the Roman empire and beyond. National Museum of Scotland, Edinburgh, from 14 November to 18 April

Beyond the Streets In spite of the title, this is very much a celebration of street art and culture starring Shepard Fairey, Goldie, Jenny Holzer and many, many more. Saatchi Gallery, London, until 5 May
Dialogues: Wilhelmina Barns-Graham x Haroun Hayward A contemporary artist goes head-to-head with the noted modernist who died in 2004. Hales Gallery, London, until 18 December

We found Tate Britain’s new exhibition, Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, an “epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings” of the co-habiting modernists. Read the full review
The brilliantly bolshie artist Ryan Gander lambasted practically everyone
Jill Posener’s cheeky, feminist photography served as a rebuttal to 80s misogyny
Epstein survivors were overwhelmed by messages of support at pop-up art exhibition
The Vatican houses a collection of Indigenous treasures questionably ‘gifted’ to it
Head of Christ Crucified by the Master of Liesborn (Johann von Soest?), probably early 1480s-1490

The blood streams over Christ’s deathly white face in a vivid, almost Hammer horror contrast between gore and pallor. It flows in thick rivulets from the crown of thorns that has been mockingly forced on to his head. The initials INRI on a piece of paper fixed to the cross stand for “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” in Latin, and the cruel crown rams home the barb. Christ bears the laughter and the physical pain with patience and dignity, lowering his eyes in sorrow as he waits for his earthly body to die. The stark, simple shock of this image comes from an age in which Europeans were encouraged to identify with Christ, to imagine themselves suffering alongside him. At the same time this artist’s explicit focus on flowing blood may serve a theological function: the central moment of the medieval Mass was the miraculous transformation of bread and wine into the actual body and blood of Christ. According to the philosopher Thomas Aquinas this took place literally: the bread and wine kept their “accidental” appearance while changing their “essential” nature. This painting is part of an altarpiece from Germany, but not all Germans were convinced by such ideas. In the early 1500s Martin Luther would rebel against the miracle of transubstantiation, and against art like this which he regarded as idolatry. National Gallery, London

items.title: Political divide threatens Kurdish autonomy; US urges unity
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Last week's withdrawal of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan from the Iraqi Kurdistan’s regional government has deepened the political standoff between the region's two main ruling parties.
The rise in tensions came after a disputed parliamentary session prompted the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) to announce its withdrawal from the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG).

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), led by the Barzani family, and the PUK, led by the Talabani family, have dominated Kurdish politics for decades. Their rivalry led to a brutal armed conflict and separate administrations in the 1990s.
Some regional analysts warn that the latest tensions could lead to a renewed division of the Kurdistan region.

"If we divide this region ourselves, the entire world will abandon us,” Kamil Omar, a university professor in Sulaimaniyah, told VOA. “How long can they continue worrying about us when we cannot protect our own region, our people’s future and our nation’s strategic interests?”
The Kurdistan Region gained de facto autonomy following the 1991 Gulf War, with its federal status recognized in Iraq’s 2005 constitution.
“We have received political and military support and protection from international allies for the past 35 years," he added.

Speaking at Chatham House in London on Wednesday, U.S. special envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack urged Kurdish leaders to overcome their “family” and “tribal” divisions and strengthen cooperation with Baghdad.
“This is an Iraqi issue. This is an Iraqi decision. This is not an American decision,” Barrack said. “My advice, the president’s advice, is: Get over it.”
Masoud Haider, a KDP member and former Iraqi deputy finance minister, described Barrack’s remarks as a clear political message urging both parties to agree on forming a government.

“A strong Kurdistan Region with unified institutions contributes to Iraq’s strength and stability,” Haider told VOA. “This message calls on Kurdish political forces to put their differences aside and form a government based on cooperation and responsibility.”
Mahmoud Khoshnaw, a PUK member, described Barrack’s remarks as both a reflection of political realities and a warning.

“Any step that promotes stability and development strengthens the region, while any step that undermines stability, creates political divisions or marginalizes a political party weakens it,” Khoshnaw told VOA.
Speaking Thursday at the Sulaimani Forum, PUK leader Bafel Talabani described the dispute as “the single largest political crisis in the history of the Kurdistan Region.”
He rejected the legitimacy of the disputed parliamentary process and warned against further unilateral moves.
“We effectively have two administrations,” Talabani said, although he cautioned that discussing two separate governments was premature.
“Every escalation will be met with a well-planned escalation,” he warned, adding that dialogue remained possible.
Talabani rejected characterizing the dispute as a family feud, describing it instead as a longstanding rivalry between two political forces.
On Monday, KDP leader Masoud Barzani called for negotiations.
“I call on our brothers in the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan to sit down with the KDP, resolve the problems and bring an end to the Kurdistan Region’s political crisis,” Barzani said in a statement.
The KRG Council of Ministers, meeting Wednesday without PUK ministers, also urged them to return and address their concerns through cabinet discussions.
Talabani dismissed those appeals as political rhetoric intended to shift blame for the divisions onto the PUK.

items.title: What we know about the global outage
paragraphs: More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming for some, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

items.title: Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme
paragraphs: For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline.

As the founder and chief executive of Nvidia resigned this week after reports of multiple affairs, his affinity for a leather jacket, an item of clothing typically associated with a man in midlife crisis mode, has become widely mocked.

The Cut ran a story suggesting a clear line between his penchant for a luxury leather jacket and his extramarital affairs. “Jensen Huang’s leather jackets confessed before he did” read the headline. Writing in the New York Times, the author Anand Giridharadas asked “is an expensive leather jacket on a middle-aged man the new symbol of a honeypot victim?”

Meanwhile, the internet is rife with memes, including an AI-generated image of a leather jacket flying at half mast outside Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. There was also another fake image, this time of Huang in a studded leather jacket, that many people believed was real.

Elsewhere, there are plenty of divorced dad jokes doing the rounds. “Jensen leather jacket discourse reminds me of the time two years ago when I wore my beloved moto jacket to a party and my good friend said “great jacket, sorry you got divorced”, wrote one user on X.

Similar to Steve Jobs’s black rollneck and jeans or Mark Zuckerberg’s Latin-sloganed T-shirts, Huang’s black leather jacket has become a visual trademark. He likes to pair a leather jacket (always black) with a black T-shirt and black jeans.

In September, in an interview with CBS, Huang explained he had 30 to 40 leather jackets. He credited his wife, Lori Huang, with choosing them. They vary from motorcycle-inspired jackets with a tighter fit and plenty of zips to collarless croc-embossed jackets and clean-cut tailored versions. He has worn them to trade shows, to parties and to give keynote speeches at developer conferences. In 2021 he appeared on the cover of Time magazine in a black leather jacket from Tom Ford. In July, another Tom Ford jacket worn and signed by Huang sold at a charity auction at Sotheby’s for $960,000, more than 10 times its original price.
“The leather jacket is Huang’s way of borrowing some cool,” says Peter Bevan, a writer and stylist. Bevan points to the leather jacket’s “rebel history” as part of the appeal.

Marlon Brando led his biker gang wearing an asymmetric zip jacket in 1953’s The Wild One; James Dean zipped around off-screen in a similar style while following his Berlin era; David Bowie wore a black leather jacket on the cover of his Heroes album in 1977. Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing, John Travolta in Grease and Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones also made a leather jacket an enduring symbol of Hollywood style.
By choosing a black leather jacket rather than a corporate suit, it suggests that Huang is unconventional, a leader rather than a conformist.
“It’s basically Huang saying: ‘I’m not a regular billionaire boss, I’m a cool billionaire boss’,” Bevan says.

When asked by CBS in October why he wore a leather jacket day in, and day out, Huang said it helped him avoid decision fatigue. “Black is the absence of choice,” he said. “It’s nice to wear the same thing every day because no surprises. For everybody else, they probably have to make three or four decisions. I took that off my plate. The moment I wake up, I could be thinking about important things.”

It’s a look that has not gone unnoticed by his fellow tech giants. In 2024, Zuckerberg posted a photo of Huang swapping jackets. Later in the year, at a Siggraph conference in Colorado, Zuckerberg presented him with another jacket. “It’s black and leather and shearling,” Zuckerberg said describing the coat. “It’s a vibe. I mean, get this guy a chain.” In return, Huang gave him the black leather jacket he was wearing, explaining that Lori had bought it for him to commemorate that year’s conference. “This is worth more because it’s used,” Zuckerberg said as he slipped it on.

Bevan says that while Huang’s choice of designer jackets are “the kind that most fashion insiders would rate”, a box-fresh leather jacket “feels try hard” and as a result, “tips into midlife crisis territory fast”.
The biggest mistake men make when buying a leather jacket Bevan says is choosing one that is “too shiny, too new and too tight.”
The list of those who get it wrong is long – including Jeremy Clarkson, who likes to wear a black leather jacket with bootcut jeans.
For Bevan, the men who have mastered a leather jacket are those who “look like they’ve owned it for ever”.

Lenny Kravitz who, like Huang, is in his 60s, prefers a battered leather jacket. John Malkovich, who is a decade older, likes a brown oversized leather jacket, while the rapper A$AP Rocky, who is in his 30s, has made a bomber leather jacket his style staple.

For those without youth or “rock-star DNA” on their side, Bevan suggests ditching a leather jacket for a cotton Harrington style that he describes as “having the same cool but none of the leather-clad midlife baggage”.

As for Huang, he may have to reconsider his default wardrobe for next week. While he managed to pull off a leather jacket at tech conferences, it may be harder to pull off at a congressional testimony.

items.title: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of UK knife attack
paragraphs: A former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.
Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.
The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.
Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year.
The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not been named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.
During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath.
He told the court he chased the bailiff across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts.
Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.
However, jurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group Hamas or his work as a bodyguard to its now-deceased former leader, Ismail Haniyeh.
While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was re-arrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in Central Europe.
Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.

When Alfatih went by the name of Naim, he enrolled in a VIP protection course and was selected to accompany Haniyeh on trips to Egypt and other countries between 2006 and 2008. However, he was later removed from the role due to his behaviour.
The second son of former Hamas health minister Bassem Naim, he later spent time in Malaysia, Qatar and Turkey before arriving in Britain.
Following his conviction, a government source said it was "staggering" that he was granted asylum and later given citizenship.
During his evidence, Alfatih did not mention Hamas, but told the court he had been tortured for 25 days while detained in Egypt in 2010.
The father-of-four, an IT worker, failed in a legal application to try to get the wounding charges thrown out on the grounds of prejudicial media coverage.
The coverage included details of allegations related to seven arrests made by German authorities, but Judge George Lubega ruled the reports did not pose a high risk of prejudice to Alfatih's trial.
During a two-week trial at Birmingham Crown Court the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.
Bailiff Kevin Bucknall was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment, but the defendant had pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.
Alfatih told jurors it happened a day after he learned one of his brothers had been killed in Gaza.
He also said while giving evidence that traumatic experiences in his past included being shot and injured on two different occasions.
"I just want to be as honest as I can," he told the jury.
"I don't think I was even in my full mind. I didn't intend anything other than him moving away.
Defence barrister Kate O'Raghallaigh said Alfatih had a heightened perception of danger, triggered by fear and desperation he had previously experienced.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours over three days before convicting him.
Sentencing will take place at a later date.
A Home Office spokesperson said Hamas was a proscribed terrorist organisation and the government condemned "those who choose to support its activities and further its aims".

items.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
paragraphs: The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.

“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US were held this week in Abu Dhabi.

Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.

European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.

The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.

Despite more than two years of on-off talks, the EU has not settled on a choice. But there is a growing view that Europe should not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent.

Paris and Berlin support a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: the European Council’s president, António Costa, and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.

Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

items.title: Trump loses control of Congress – level 1
paragraphs: The Democrats win a big election in the US. They now control Congress. President Donald Trump and his team lose many votes.

Now, people in both political parties are fighting about what to do next. Vice President JD Vance says that the war with Iran is a bad idea. Many people do not like Trump anymore because of that. Trump said that his immigration rules are too hard. But he still puts his immigration leader in a top job. At the same time, Democrats are trying to agree on new plans for the country.
Experts think that it will still be very hard for leaders in Washington to pass new laws and help people quickly.

Difficult words: vote (when a person formally chooses a person in an election), immigration rules (what people who come from other countries must and must not do), pass (to officially say yes to a new rule).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Trump loses control of Congress – level 2
paragraphs: The Democratic Party won big in the US midterm elections and took control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

This defeat caused strong arguments inside both parties. Vice President JD Vance blamed the election loss on the war with Iran, and disagreed directly with Trump. At the same time, Trump said his strict immigration rules went too far, but he still chose the creator of those rules to lead his White House team. Meanwhile, Democrats are fighting over their plans, as its members want different things.

Experts say that even with new Democratic leaders in Congress, it will be hard to pass major new laws because the president can still block them, which may lead to more political delays in Washington.

Difficult words: defeat (the loss of a contest, game, election, or battle), blame (to say or think that someone or something is responsible for something bad that happened), major (important, big, serious).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Trump loses control of Congress – level 3
paragraphs: Following a decisive defeat in the US midterm elections, Donald Trump and the Republican Party have lost control of both houses of Congress to the Democrats. The results have sparked intense disputes within both major parties.

Among Republicans, Vice President JD Vance has attributed the electoral losses to the unpopular war with Iran, which created a visible rift with the president. At the same time, Donald Trump has sent mixed signals regarding his policy direction: while publicly acknowledging that his strict immigration enforcement went too far, he appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of those policies, as White House Chief of Staff. On the Democratic side, progressives and moderates are competing to shape the party’s future legislative agenda.

Political analysts warn that despite the significant shift in congressional control, deep ideological divisions and the president’s veto power will likely lead to continued political gridlock in Washington rather than major policy changes.

Difficult words: dispute (a disagreement, argument, or debate between people, parties, or groups), rift (a serious break in friendly relations between people or groups), gridlock (a situation where no progress can be made because of strong disagreement or opposing forces).
You can watch the video news lower on this page.
