items.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
paragraphs: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

items.title: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
paragraphs: As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.
"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."
However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.

items.title: Texas antique and design show unveils new exhibition building made from salvaged materials
paragraphs: Texas-based antique and design show Marburger Farm has unveiled an exhibition building made partly from salvaged materials sourced directly from across the 43-acre property, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Called Gage Hall, the building’s facade is made from reclaimed timber sourced from around the farm and is topped with a traditional Texas metal roof and contemporary skylight elements that bring natural light into the hall.

The hall brings an additional 7,500 square feet of shopping space to Marburger Farm, bringing the fair’s total space to 100,000 square feet. Designed to honour the site’s dairy farm heritage, the hall also showcases its vision for the future.
The antique and design show has become a destination for international designers looking to source unique interior objects including furniture, lighting and vintage textiles.
The 43-acre show is located in Round Top, Texas, and has attracted designers such as Kelly Wearstler and Leanne Ford.
The fair offers visitors access to objects from over 200 independent dealers and has become one of the largest antique shows in the United States.
The site also includes a Texas-style town square, 10 restored historic buildings, four tents and a 150-year-old saloon, which has been restored to its original use as a social space and bar.
Founded in 1997, the show has grown to attract over 30,000 people annually.
The antique show takes place in January, March and October each year.
Marburger Farm is owned by Brook Partners, a Dallas-based investment company focusing on culture and commerce.
The company also runs the upcoming Dallas Art Fair, which is held from 15 to 18 April 2027 in Dallas, Texas. To learn more, visit the Marburger Farm website.

Marburger Farm Antique Show took place from 27 to 31 October in Round Top, Texas. The winter show will take place 21-24 January and the spring show will take place 23-27 March 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
This video was produced by Dezeen as part of a partnership with Marburger Farm. Find out more about Dezeen partnership content here.
Photography by Marburger Farm and Ethan Good Photography

items.title: Does Nvidia need a new logo as well as a new CEO?
paragraphs: Today, the Nvidia logo is recognised not only by dedicated gamers and creatives interested in the best graphics cards for video editing. The company's stock performance has turned it into a household name, while the demand for computer components amid the AI boom has ensured that a new headline is never far away.

Alas, it turns out that the DLSS 5 controversy is the least of its problems. Former CEO Jensen Huang has now resigned after embroiling Nvidia in a honeytrap scandal worthy of a spy novel. CFO Colette Kress has stepped up as interim CEO and an executive search has begun.
But the debacle has also resurfaced another question. Why does one of the world's most valuable companies still have such a terrible logo design? And could this be the moment for a refresh?
See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

Over on Reddit, designers are debating the "least aesthetically pleasing, most poorly designed corporate logo" still in use today, and the Nvidia logo is the example that was used to get the ball rolling. Other contenders put forward on the thread include the X logo and, of course, the infamous Kia logo.

I can see where the OP is coming from. Nvidia was the world's most valuable company until the Jensen Huang honeytrap controversy hammered its share price and put Apple back in the lead on the Nasdaq. The identities of those two companies couldn't look or feel more different. The Apple logo is sleek and minimalist. It feels modern and premium. The Nvidia logo is... weird.

"So many things I hate about this design: The Aztec-looking spiral eye, the half inverted color, the lime green, black, and white color pallette, the '80s sci-fi font. None of it coheres well," the OP writes on Reddit.

Of course, Apple and Nvidia are very different beasts. Apple is mainly consumer facing and Nvidia's business is mainly corporate. On the consumer side, Nvidia's GPUs are packaged and sold by other brands rather than by Nvidia directly. But the company is becoming much more of a household name as its tentacles spread.

Nvidia components are being promoted more visibly in GeForce RTX laptops, and the company's being collaborating on workflow developments with creative software developers like Adobe, Blackmagic (DaVinci Resolve) and the Blender Foundation.
There is a compelling case for a change. Nvidia's visual identity was born in a very different age of technology back in 1993. Its last logo redesign was twenty years ago in 2006.

Time alone is never a reason for a rebrand, even for a tech company. IBM's had the same logo since 1972. But with Nvidia, the age shows. The wonky eye, brat green colour palette and retro-futuristic type feel rooted in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when aggressive, futuristic aesthetics dominated PC hardware branding.
Compared with the cleaner, more restrained identities of companies like Apple, Microsoft, OpenAI and even AMD, Nvidia's main rival in the GPU space, the branding feels tied to gaming origins.

There's also a somewhat dark occult reference going on. In the company's name, the 'NV' comes from the shorthand that was used to identify the 'next version' in file names, while the 'invidia' part means 'envy' in Latin.

That feeling will be familiar to anyone who has a colleague with an RTX 5090, but it's a strange choice for a brand. The word is often associated with malice and the 'evil eye' and was sometimes used as the Roman name for the ancient Greek deity, Nemesis, the personification of divine retribution. Yikes.

Today, the firm's influence and ambitions extend far beyond GeForce. It sells AI infrastructure, networking technology, autonomous vehicle platforms and enterprise computing systems. A more refined visual identity could reflect its status as a global AI platform rather than a 'mere' component manufacturer.

That said, for all of its weirdness, Nvidia's mysterious green eye is one of the most distinctive marks in tech. A rebrand could risk of abandoning something that has aged better than critics might admit.

While the eye doesn't feel especially contemporary, it is unique. At a time when many companies are converging towards minimalist sans-serif wordmarks and simplified geometric symbols, the identity stands out precisely because it has character, and distinctiveness is arguably more valuable than modernity.

The strongest argument would probably be for a careful evolution. The company could modernise the typography and tweak the eye. It might be able to find a more appealing shade of green. A relatively subtle refresh could preserve decades of recognition while signalling that Nvidia has entered a new chapter.

But it remains to be seen how much the last two weeks have changed things. It looked like Jensen Huang was going to hang on until yesterday's resignation announcement. The company might also decide that the controversy requires a clear visual break from the past.
There's plenty of branding inspiration about this week that Nvidia might want to check out, from the solid Caixa rebrand in Brazil to the intriguing new Takara Tomy logo .
Let me know below if you agree that Nvidia has the worst corporate logo in tech, or if you feel that there's a stronger candidate.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: A baffling trail from Australia to Singapore: what is Megaspeed, the company implicated in downfall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
paragraphs: A lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur, and a near-empty office in Singapore: the global facades of Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, form a puzzling corporate picture.

The company, which is registered in Singapore, has registered affiliates across the US, Asia and Australia, but individuals at its offices say they know nothing about the cloud computing firm at the centre of a global spy scandal.

On Friday Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees. US intelligence agencies believe Huang had been targeted by Alice Huang (no relation), the former director of Megaspeed International.
US officials believe Huang was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported.
On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Alice Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company.

Singapore police said last October they were investigating Megaspeed over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” after a US senator requested the commerce department investigate whether the firm had diverted Nvidia chips.

The ministry of home affairs said this week it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” related to Megaspeed. Eventually, she was released with a stern warning.
Earlier this week, authorities in Taiwan said she had also been barred from re-entering there.
On Friday Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.
Across the region, Megaspeed’s activities remain obscure.

In Sydney, no signage, mailbox or physical presence suggests the company at the epicentre of one of the biggest stories in the world is located on the 10th floor of an office building in the city centre.

“Do you have an appointment?” a receptionist asked when the Guardian visted the office, home to numerous businesses. It hummed with activity but no one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.

Megaspeed International filed papers in the US state of Delaware ⁠and with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic), showing the affiliates were created in 2024. Both filings list the Shanghai-born Kang as the sole company officer, either as ​director or president.
The Australian ‌filing also lists the Singapore-based parent as ‌the company’s stockholder.
A woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said she had run the business for about 16 years. She said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.
“He doesn’t have any business here,” she said, adding that Kang had completed his master’s degree at Shanghai University.
He had visited his parents most recently in August and September, she said.
She said she knew about Nvidia and Megaspeed but her son had nothing to do with the company in Singapore.

It is not the only perplexing finding that journalists have encountered when trying to track down representatives of Megaspeed, which in the past three years has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware.

The Straits Times reported that Swiftdata, the little-known company that owns Megaspeed, had a registered business address in Singapore, but an interior design firm said it had occupied the premises for more than four years.
Last year the New York Times visited Megaspeed’s Singapore headquarters, located in the central business district, but found only two employees present.

And in neighbouring Malaysia, the Times found that one of Megaspeed’s offices was a dilapidated storefront in the capital. Another was located in a shopping mall. When one employee emerged in the mall, she was asked what the company did.
Kang is also registered as a director in Megaspeed’s Malaysian, Indonesian and Thai units.
Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.

In Australia, a former intelligence officer said they expected Australian security agencies would have sought briefings from overseas counterparts about Megaspeed or undertaken their own assessments of the local subsidiary this week.

Michael Shoebridge, the director of the security thinktank Strategic Analysis Australia and a former deputy of the Australian Signals Directorate and the Defence Intelligence Organisation (Asio), said key details about Megaspeed’s relationship with Chinese intelligence remained unclear.
He suggested it would be “credible” to assess the company as a “front for Chinese intelligence” but nothing was certain.

The Chinese government has flatly rejected any claims Alice Huang was a spy. A foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said earlier this week the allegations were “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China”.
Shoebridge said Megaspeed’s Australian operation could be a legitimate business or designed to make the Singapore-based parent company “look credible” by having overseas affiliates.
Asio declined to comment when asked if it was examining Megaspeed Australia. The office of the Australian home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also declined to comment.

The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, was asked on ABC TV this week whether there had been discussions inside government “about some of the potential spying that could be taking place within Australian companies”.

On ABC radio, Marles, speaking generally, said: “We are living in a world where there is more espionage than there has been for a long time. A lot of that is particularly around emerging technologies.”
The federal opposition said any potential foreign interference “must be taken seriously”.
An email to the Victorian newsagent and messages to its Facebook page requesting comment went unanswered on Thursday.

Asic documents show Kang was born in 1996 in Shanghai and has been listed as Megaspeed Australia’s director since the company was registered. They reveal Megaspeed International owns all 10,000 shares of Megaspeed Australia’s stocks, for which it paid $1m.

items.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
paragraphs: Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the owners.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.
Community drop-in sessions about the vision, external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.
Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

items.title: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw me
paragraphs: Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made her life "hell" at times
As a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.
At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.
Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.
As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable".
"Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.
Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts".
"I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.
Charlie didn't tell her parents about the severity of her condition for years

The condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.
Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.
Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.

The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".
But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.
It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits".
If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.
But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.
Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety".
"It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."
That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.
Charlie wants to raise awareness of the condition
A breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.
Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.
What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17.
"I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said.
"It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied.
"It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."
McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.
Niall McGonigle was inspired to become a surgeon after his experience with a pectus deformity
"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said.
"If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services.
"But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."
McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.
Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.
She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister.
"I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.
Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.
A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.
It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.
One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.
It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.
Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.
In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".
It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery".
"The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."
Vacuum bell therapy is a non-surgical treatment that works best for younger people
Last month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.
Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term.
"If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."

items.title: Victoria election 2026: Labor and Greens trade accusations of ‘dodgy deals’ as preference fight puts key seats at risk
paragraphs: The Greens have retaliated against Labor’s decision to run an open ticket in a key inner-city seat by refusing to direct preferences to the party in 15 electorates across the state at this month’s Victorian election.
The move has sparked a war of words between the two parties, with each accusing the other of striking a “dodgy deal” that could help the Liberals and One Nation get elected on 28 November.
On Friday, the Greens confirmed they would only be directing voters to number the Greens one and One Nation last across 15 electorates.

The decision follows Labor’s decision on Tuesday to run an open ticket in the inner Melbourne seat of Prahran, where the Greens had been counting on Labor preferences to win it back. It has been held by the Liberals on a tiny 1.3% margin – after the Greens lost it at a byelection in 2025.
At the time, the Victorian Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, told Guardian Australia that Labor’s “unforgivable” decision could hand the upcoming election to a Liberal-One Nation coalition.
A Labor spokesperson turned the accusation back on the Greens on Friday, mirroring Sandell’s language.
“In one of the most consequential elections in Victoria’s history – the Greens have done a dodgy deal to help elect a Liberal-One Nation government,” the spokesperson said.

“This is unforgivable and Victorians won’t forget it’s Ellen Sandell and the Greens to blame when Jess Wilson cuts our hospitals and schools – and One Nation winds back our nation leading reforms on women’s rights and Treaty.”
The Greens responded by accusing Labor of “lying to Victorian voters”.
“The Greens will be putting One Nation last in every single electorate across Victoria,” their spokesperson said. “We always encourage people to vote in line with their values.
“After months of scaremongering about a Liberal-One Nation government, it is Labor who have done a dodgy backroom deal with the Liberals that could help elect one.”

The 15 electorates where the Greens will issue these how-to-vote cards are: Albert Park, Ashwood, Bellarine, Bendigo East, Bendigo West, Essendon, Euroa, Gippsland East, Mildura, Mornington, Point Cook, Polwarth, South Barwon, Tarneit and Werribee.

Labor fears the decision will particularly hurt their chances in Albert Park, Ashwood, Bellarine, South Barwon and the two Bendigo seats vacated by former premier Jacinta Allan and speaker Maree Edwards.
The Coalition is quietly confident it is improving its chances of fending off One Nation and snatching seats from Labor.

However, Tony Barry, the Liberal strategist turned pollster with Redbridge and co-host of Guardian Australia’s Back to Back Barries podcast, said most Greens voters don’t closely follow their party’s how-to-vote cards.

“Historical preference flows from past state and federal elections shows about 85% of exhausted Greens votes flow to Labor and about 15% leakage to the Coalition, and that rarely changes regardless of the particular circumstances,” Barry said.

But he said in Essendon, where Labor candidate Kat Theodosis is contesting the seat following Danny Pearson’s retirement, in a complex race involving the Liberals, One Nation and three independents candidates, it “might be enough to flip the seat to the Liberals.”

Meanwhile, the conservative Family First party is directing its preferences to Labor candidates affiliated with the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association (SDA), placing them second on their how-to-vote cards.
The cards feature an image of a baby next to the Labor candidate name with claims they have a “pro-life voting record”.

It prompted Pasoce Vale MP Anthony Cianflone, who is in a tight race against the Greens’ Angelica Panopoulos, to post a statement on social media saying he supported “women’s right to make their own decisions about their bodies and healthcare”.
“That’s why I have supported the Victorian Labor government’s reforms protecting these rights,” Cianflone said.
Family First have also preferenced Matthew Guy last in his safe Liberal seat of Bulleen.

The Family First state leader, Moira Deeming, was disendorsed as a Liberal candidate after alleging Guy had placed her in a headlock earlier this year. Deeming later conceded she misunderstood the technical meaning of “headlock”.

items.title: Whatever happened to the $300,000 diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
paragraphs: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.

They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.

While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.

Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.

In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.

He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.

"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.

"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.

"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.

His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.

"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.

"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."

Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

items.title: Firms help migrants pose as artists and tech experts for 'Global Talent' visas, BBC finds
paragraphs: Things would be made to look like our undercover reporter had been an artist for some time, said Peter (pictured)
ByBilly Kenberpolitics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemppolitics reporter
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.
The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.
Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.
We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.
No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.
In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.
A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.
"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.
Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.
The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.
A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".
They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.
Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.
Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media
During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:
At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying
The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application
For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.
The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.
A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."
An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".
Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".
The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.
About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.
The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.
Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".
We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent
Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.
"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.
Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.
Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.
During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.
Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.
The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.
It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.
Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.
This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.
Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.
The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.
The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.
The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal
During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.
The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.
"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."
He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".
When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.
"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".
"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."
The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".
Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.
The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.
The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".
It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.
Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.
"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."
Part of the article, including artwork purporting to be by Silva Ndifon, that Molara Wood did not write
Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.
Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.
The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.
Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.
If you would like to contact our team about this story you can email on: politicsinvestigations@bbc.co.uk, external

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 1
paragraphs: One million people come to see Pope Leo at night in Argentina. The Pope talks to many young people. He asks them to be kind. He tells them not to worry only about money, online popularity, or good looks.

Many happy people wave their phones and bring their babies for a blessing. The pope is visiting three countries in South America to talk about God and help poor people. He also asks the country’s leader to help people who do not have much money.
Many young people are very happy to see the pope and listen to his words.
Difficult words: popularity (when many people like someone), wave (to move your hand when you are saying hello to someone), blessing (a time when people ask for God’s help).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 2
paragraphs: Pope Leo spoke to a crowd of one million people during a night event in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He told young people not to focus only on money, physical appearance, or getting likes on social media.

This gathering was part of his 12-day trip through South America, which also includes visits to Uruguay and Peru. Large crowds came to see the pope, including 2.5 million people at a historic Mass earlier in the week.

Pope Leo is visiting Argentina to support Catholic followers and help poor communities. During his trip, he also asked Argentina’s president not to hurt poor people with government spending cuts. Many residents and students thanked the pope for caring about people in need.

Difficult words: physical appearance (the external, visible features of a person), gathering (when many people meet together for a specific event), cut (reduction made to financial spending, resources, or services).

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 3
paragraphs: Pope Leo drew a crowd of one million people at a nighttime vigil in Buenos Aires on Tuesday during his 12-day South American tour.

The pontiff addressed the gathered youth, urged them not to be consumed by the pursuit of wealth, physical appearance, or social media popularity, and warned against humiliating others online. This event followed an outdoor Mass in Cordoba earlier that day, which attracted 650,000 attendees, and a record-breaking gathering of 2.5 million people in Buenos Aires on Monday.

As the first pope to visit Catholic-majority Argentina since 1987, Leo seeks to revitalize the Church’s presence in the region against growing evangelical competition. Throughout his visit, the US-born pope has also voiced strong criticism of Argentine President Javier Milei’s strict austerity policies. He argued that government spending cuts disproportionately harm the country’s poorest citizens.

Difficult words: pontiff (the Pope, who acts as the chief bishop and leader of the Roman Catholic Church), pursuit (chasing or striving to achieve something), austerity (severity in government spending cutbacks and financial discipline).
You can watch the video news lower on this page.
