items.title: ‘You can almost smell the sweat’: striptease artists and steel pans light up this week’s free art shows
paragraphs: A vast red concrete wall splits Maxwell Alexandre’s work in two. It’s the wall of the Flamengo sport club in the painter’s native Rio de Janeiro, a towering crimson monolith of division, literally separating us and them, rich and poor, black and white.

Alexandre joined the upmarket club in the early 2020s. He’d walked past its red walls countless times as a kid – the club is on the edge of the favela he’s from, the biggest in Brazil. What he found inside was serenity, sunbathing, prosperity, and whiteness. He’d spent his early career painting the black figures of his favela, but now he was surrounded by pasty bodies with rippling pink skin.

With success in his career, he’d bought access to this new world, and knew he couldn’t paint the same black figures he’d made his name with. So this is the result, dozens of paintings of lush tropical trees and white bodies in repose, lounging, chatting, playing by the pool within the confines of that red well, all part of his new approach to what he calls “white figuration”.

The red walls dominate the works in the first space as a figure stands on a diving board and palm fronds wave in the distance. The second room is covered floor to ceiling in paintings on brown paper of the club’s members, some shown next to figures from art history. Boys stand in the sun, men splash in the water, girls talk and women sunbathe. It’s idyllic, hazy, almost nostalgic painting.

But it’s full of emotional complexity. The work is a rejection of the expectations placed on black artists to make black work, to churn out paintings of black figures to sell to white audiences and collectors. It’s Alexandre refusing to play the game. But there’s also an introspective exploration of what happens when your life changes, when you stop being young and poor and desperate and become something different. This doesn’t feel like Alexandre mocking white flabby bodies, it feels like him trying to make sense of a divided city, an art history that doesn’t represent him, and a world that expects you to be something you no longer are. It all looks like heaven, but even heaven is a complicated place.
Carlos/Ishikawa, London, until 28 November

The exhaustion in Susan Meiselas’s photos is so palpable it’s almost draining. She spent three years in the mid-70s following a group of striptease performers as they toured the endless American sprawl, slowly gaining their trust, capturing them at their most intimate, unguarded and knackered.

She photographs them from backstage. Night after night the women dance seductively for wide-eyed, drooling, dumbstruck men – you see them gawping from between the dancers’ legs, anonymous pervs desperate for an eyeful.
And then the dancers crash from the effort of it all. They smoke distractedly, lounge on sofas or crumple into bed. This is the end result of physical labour: total collapse, utter exhaustion.
In lots of the photos dancers peek through the curtain back on to the stage, waiting their turn, watching things turn ugly for the poor performer on stage.

The more posed images don’t give the viewer much, but when Meiselas captures the dancers unaware, lost in the moment, they’re pretty special. These are stories of exploitation and entertainment, work and exhaustion, leaving behind nothing but physical, emotional depletion.
Huxley Parlour Photographs, London, until 21 November

Hyun-Sook Song says so much with so little. With just a handful of brushstrokes, the Hamburg-based Korean painter opens up a whole world: written into every mark are her memories of life in deeply rural, mid-century South Korea, her shock at the monstrous urbanity of modern Germany, her desperate need to find sanctuary in painting.

The minimalism of the whole thing is made obvious by the titles. The works are called things like 11 Brushstrokes or 6 Brushstrokes over 1 Brushstroke because that’s all they are, but they’re more complex than that implies.

She lays each canvas flat first, and paints every mark in a long, sweeping, full-body motion, physically trying to communicate her ideas into the work. The paintings are all on dark green or black backgrounds, each swooping brushstroke creating a gossamer white veil across the darkness. Cutting across almost all of them is a brown line, a stick that seems to almost lift the impossibly thin curtains. The white marks reference the raw silks collected in her youth, the brown marks nod to boundary posts that delineated her childhood landscapes. There are all these ideas of separation and division, of veils being lifted, of quiet and peace. They’re almost unbearably fragile paintings, but all the more beautiful and meditative for it.
Sprüth Magers, London, until 23 January 2027

Way before London’s Carnaby Street was one the capital’s main tourist taps, it was a proper cultural hub, a place for fashion and music to flourish. And No 50 Carnaby Street was home to six different music venues between the 1930s and 80s which helped totally change the cultural landscape of the country. Whether it was the Sunset Club in the 50s or Columbo’s in the 70s, this address is where activism met music, where jazz gave way to steel bands and sound systems, where black met white.

This tiny show in Sadie Coles’ downstairs project space by Studio/Chapple gallery celebrates 50 Carnaby Street just around the corner from the original address. The walls are painted deep brown, handmade speakers by Maya Ramnarine play out the sounds of old jazz and ska records, paintings show dancers moving in tightly crowded spaces, performers playing to packed rooms. I don’t love all the works here, but the idea is good, and the two paintings by Georgia Semple and Amida Deen are great. Semple’s is a dark, atmospheric vision of the Russ Henderson Steel Band, Britain’s first steel pan ensemble, playing to a crowd of joyful figures slowly swaying to the music. Deen’s work travels to the 1970s, with people pressing themselves together in a room of fiery red and heat-soaked orange as dub pours out of the speakers.
The show is a tiny love letter to music history, clubbing and dancing. You can almost smell the sweat.

items.title: Licht Kunst Licht illuminates Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade with "largely invisible" lights
paragraphs: Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht has used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

Licht Kunst Licht (LKL) collaborated with RheinEnergie and the Dombauhütte Köln restoration workshop to develop a lighting concept for Cologne‘s historic cathedral, which is also Germany’s most visited landmark.

Prior to the intervention, it was primarily illuminated using floodlights placed atop nearby buildings. These 1,000-watt metal halide lamps consumed a great deal of energy and, according to LKL, flooded the building in an unflattering neutral white light.

LKL replaced this broad-brush approach with discreet, warm-spectrum LED fixtures, illuminating the building’s Gothic features by providing subtle backlighting combined with vertical grazing light to enliven the ornate facades.
“The central concept ‘light follows architecture’ replaces indiscriminate floodlighting with targeted illumination,” the studio explained.
“Instead of flattening the facade, light is directed to articulate depth, rhythm and verticality. The outcome is a sculptural night presence while the luminaires remain largely invisible by day.”

The project’s key innovation was the development of bespoke, multifunctional lighting poles that are covertly integrated into the structure using custom clamps to protect the stonework. The aim was to render the fixtures “largely invisible” during the day and allow them to be dismantled without impacting the historic structure.
Each pole contains a glare-free light module used to provide facade or circulation lighting that is fully dimmable and can be adapted to events, seasons and ecological needs.

According to lighting designer and LKL project lead Philipp Schmitz, a lack of detailed architectural plans necessitated an extensive study of the facades to ensure the intricate Gothic details were suitably illuminated.

“Because digital simulations were insufficient for such a complex, heterogeneous structure, we conducted years of extensive on-site lighting tests, experimenting with optics, angles and positions to achieve the desired effects through empirical observation,” he pointed out.

Only 10 per cent of the light now comes from fixtures located away from the building, compared to 80 per cent previously. This reduces unwanted light scatter and improves precision, while long-wave light reduces disruption to nocturnal species.
A series of minimalist stainless-steel lighting pylons on the cathedral plaza now illuminate entrances and highlight selected facade elements.
Sustainability was a key consideration throughout the project, with overall energy consumption reduced by 80 per cent while delivering improved visual quality, according to LKL.
Cologne Cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Cologne and is a renowned monument of German Catholicism and Gothic architecture.

Construction began in 1248 but was halted around 1560 and then restarted in the 19th century, with the building finally completed to its original medieval plan in 1880. The cathedral, which was briefly the world’s tallest building upon its completion, went on to be declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

Dezeen readers crowned LKL’s scheme lighting design of the year in the public vote at this year’s Dezeen Awards. The project is now in the running to be crowned overall winner by a jury of leading industry figures including Norman Foster, Michael Anastassiades and Jaime Hayon.

items.title: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?
paragraphs: Councils across England own hundreds of thousands artworks, but what are they doing with it all?
Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.
More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.
Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.
Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.
Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.
Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.
Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.
As of April, just 26,856 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?
Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.
All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.
Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities.
"If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said.
"It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."
Sally Godden said the museum team aimed to ensure the council collection instilled "pride in the people of Rugby"

Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset.

"We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."
The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.
Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.
Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.
The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of.
For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools.
When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.
Rugby, which is among the councils adding to their collections, recently acquired a painting selected by students and pupils living in the town
Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April.
At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept.
"I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."
The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.

The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".
Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks, external.
Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art.
"We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place.
"The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time.
"From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it."
He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.
Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.
But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".
Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26.
Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.
Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.
One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum.
Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.
Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public.
That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.
It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.
Mark Doyle said it was "fair to say that when we reopen, there will be more of the collections on display at any one time than there ever has been"
Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme.
"We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."
Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council.
"A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.
Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time.

"Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment."
Additional reporting by Lauren Woodhead and Jonathan Fagg.

items.title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
paragraphs: Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).

The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.

PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.

The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer., external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.

The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.

The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.

The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.
"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.
One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.

items.title: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns
paragraphs: Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
Although the technology can help fight crime, the report found it is beset by errors and biases, and operators do not always realise they must make further inquiries to verify the data.

The report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary, published on Wednesday, covers only retrospective facial recognition. The technology is seen as less controversial and less tricky to get right than live facial recognition, which is used in real time to find suspects.
“Some investigators didn’t know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence and required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action,” the report said.
“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”
The report said there are still issues with bias in the algorithm, including being more likely to wrongly flag people from ethnic minorities as suspects.

It said: “More needs to be done to reduce the risks of people being wrongly arrested … Auditors also identified cases where users uploaded poor-quality or unsuitable probe images, including blurred images and images containing multiple faces. These factors reduced the system’s ability to return reliable matches.”
Inspectors also found a risk of public confidence being undermined because custody images that should have been deleted were in fact kept.

The report says: “Inspectors found that legislation hasn’t kept up with changes in facial recognition technology and there is no comprehensive statutory framework governing this technology’s use. This makes it more difficult for forces to understand the lawful basis for RFR’s use and what safeguards are needed to protect the public.”

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly: “Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment. A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”
Facial recognition is seen by police chiefs as the next big leap forward in crime fighting, and next huge threat to civil liberties by sceptics.
Jasleen Chaggar, from Big Brother Watch, said: “The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming.

“This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they’ve never visited, as we’ve seen before.

“Worse still, police aren’t even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without even realising why they’ve been accused.

“Police cannot be allowed to continue using the algorithm with so few safeguards and at biased settings that are more likely to misidentify women, Asian and black people and search against millions of unlawfully held custody images.”

Ben Russell, lead on facial recognition for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said: “Policing remains committed to the ethical, proportionate and responsible use of retrospective facial recognition to help investigate crime, bring offenders to justice and keep communities safe and we are pleased that HMICFRS has recognised the exciting possibilities of this technology.”

Prof Pete Fussey of the University of Southampton, formerly a police adviser on facial recognition, said: “Meaningful human scrutiny of AI systems is a legal requirement, yet the report gives examples of investigators taking the computer’s suggestions at face value without further checks.”

items.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
paragraphs: Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.

The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.

Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.

The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

items.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
paragraphs: Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, external, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, external, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture, external.
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires, and overheating," said Fisher.

Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.
"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.
This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.
Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.
"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.
"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."
She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.
When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".
She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.
Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.
"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.
"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.
"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."
She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.
Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.
"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.
The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".
"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.

The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing £200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.
"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

items.title: Elliptic analytics say North Korea launders stolen Binance funds via homemade meme coins
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

North Korea is laundering cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through homemade meme coins, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, describing it as a scheme designed to resemble ordinary trading and delay investigators.
The FBI on October 31 attributed the theft of than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from Binance to North Korea.
North Korea Pyongyang has denied being involved but the FBI says it has identified this specific “North Korean malicious” cyber activity as "TraderTraitor."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
In its November 9 analysis, Elliptic said those laundering the funds created at least six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain between November 5 and November 7.
About 117,000 NEAR — worth approximately $430,000 at the time of the analysis — passed through them.
Meme coins are tokens inspired by internet jokes, animals, or celebrities, with prices driven by online attention and speculation.
Elliptic assessed that these tokens have no apparent practical purpose other than to move funds within the laundering network.

Elliptic says the launderers created exchange pools holding their tokens and NEAR wallets that contain stolen NEAR, while other wallets in the network sold the same tokens into those pools and collected NEAR.

This replaced direct transfers between wallets with purchases and sales, potentially making recipients look like investors earning legitimate trading profits. Elliptic said network wallets conducted all sales of the six tokens. They were traded intensively soon after creation, with no trading since November 8. Each cost about $90 to create.

All transactions remain publicly recorded on the blockchain, enabling investigators to trace them. But additional steps take time to unravel, helping launderers move funds before the associated wallets are identified, and transactions can be blocked, Elliptic said.
The Binance theft occurred October 29 across 11 blockchains. Elliptic estimates losses at $6.43 billion, which is the largest cryptocurrency theft ever, according to the FBI.
Elliptic’s November 9 update put conversions into bitcoin at approximately $225 million, with $2.85 billion frozen or seized and roughly $3 billion remaining in theft-linked addresses.

items.title: Moolenaar urges next Congress to continue bipartisan China committee amid questions over its future
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement released November 9, urged the next Congress to renew the panel’s mandate, saying it should continue its bipartisan work on China policy when lawmakers return early next year.

Moolenaar said the select committee had brought Republicans and Democrats together over nearly four years to address what he described as serious threats posed by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to American interests and values.

"For nearly four years the Select Committee has brought together Republicans and Democrats to address the grave threats the Chinese Communist Party poses to U.S. interests and values," Moolenaar said. "We have worked hand-in-hand with other committees and administrations of both parties to secure vital policy changes that strengthen our nation and protect the American people."

The Michigan Republican said the committee had exposed the CCP's exploitation of the U.S. economy, American workers, and innovators. He also highlighted its bipartisan efforts to secure critical supply chains, deny Beijing access to resources and technologies needed to advance what he called its dangerous ambitions, and advocate for people fighting for freedom and dignity.

Moolenaar warned that the challenges facing the United States were becoming increasingly urgent, particularly as technological competition in artificial intelligence intensifies and China's coercive actions against U.S. allies and partners continue to escalate.
“The coming two years will be a critical period—and an opportunity to meet the moment through the Select Committee’s bipartisan mandate and work."
History of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

The Select Committee on China was established in January 2023, during the 118th Congress, after Republicans gained a majority in the House of Representatives in the 2022 midterm elections.The committee was created under House Resolution 11, introduced by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-California). The resolution passed the House on January 10, 2023, by an overwhelming bipartisan vote of 365 to 65, with 146 Democrats joining all but absent Republican members in supporting its creation.

Its creation reflected growing bipartisan concern in Washington over China's expanding economic, technological, military, and geopolitical influence, as well as the implications of the Chinese Communist Party's policies for U.S. national security and economic competitiveness.

Unlike a traditional standing committee, the Select Committee on China was established as a temporary investigative and policy-focused panel. Its mandate was to build bipartisan consensus on the challenges posed by the CCP and develop policy recommendations to counter these threats.
The 120th Congress is scheduled to convene on January 3, 2027, when newly elected lawmakers will be sworn into office.

items.title: Russian prosecutors seek 15-year prison sentence for lawyer Maria Bontsler in treason case
paragraphs: Editor's note: This story was adapted from the original VOA Russian article.
Russian Prosecutors have asked a court to sentence Kaliningrad lawyer Maria Bontsler to 15 years in prison on charges of high treason.
Bontsler is known for representing defendants in politically sensitive cases. She was detained in late May 2025 and has remained in pre-trial detention ever since.

Slovo Zashchite, translated in English as "A Word to the Defense," first reported the news, citing attorney Ilya Sidorov, who visited Bontsler in pretrial detention. Sidorov was on Bontsler's defense team until July 2026, when he was removed from the case.
Bontsler could deliver her final statement in court Wednesday before the verdict is handed down.
She was initially accused of confidential cooperation with a foreign state. Investigators say Bontsler passed information about Russian security officers to Ukraine’s SBU security service.
Authorities later reclassified the case as high treason, a charge that carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years under Russian law.
She is currently being held in a detention center in Kaliningrad, and according to Bontsler's lawyer, her health has deteriorated in prison due to complications related to diabetes and hypertension.
Valeria Vetoshkina, a lawyer with the independent human rights group OVD-Info, told VOA that Bontsler's physical condition remains a major concern.

"Unfortunately, she is not feeling well. Everyone knows that Russian detention facilities and prisons are extremely difficult places. People are often treated poorly, and adequate medical care is frequently unavailable."
Human rights advocates have repeatedly expressed concern about Bontsler's health and the conditions of her detention as she awaits the outcome of her trial.

"If a person has chronic illnesses, they can worsen significantly in custody, and that is what happened in her case," Vetoshkina said. "She lost consciousness at one point and was not provided with proper medical assistance."
Vetoshkina also said she "would not be surprised if the sentence is close to what prosecutors are seeking."
Treason cases can carry a life sentence. But Russian law prohibits life imprisonment for women, so according to Vetoshkina, "the maximum punishment is 20 years."
The human rights lawyer also highlighted an unusually harsh approach by local security services.

"It appears that the local Federal Security Service (FSB) has taken a particular interest in this case. We see an extraordinary level of severity and a very negative attitude toward her," she said. "Given everything that has happened, I would not be surprised if the final sentence is close to the term being requested by prosecutors."
Vetoshkina also pointed out that Bontsler had frequently defended people prosecuted in cases initiated by the local FSB.

items.title: Adobe MAX 2026 Sneaks: Project Link Up is making design playful again
paragraphs: Sneaks is often the highlight of Adobe MAX, giving the brand an opportunity to share the exciting innovations it's working on. Among the wild Adobe Sneaks announced today, one tool in particular could be game-changing for a whole host of creatives, from illustrators to concept artists, marking an exciting upcoming era for the brand.

Project Link Up is set to revolutionise vector design, turning the simple dragging function into context-aware fusion that automatically matches a scene's perspective. (TLDR: constantly redrawing objects at new viewing angles could soon be a thing of the past).

To understand more about Project Link Up, I caught up with Hailin Jin, senior principal scientist and research lead for imaging and design at Adobe, to get his behind-the-scenes insight into the work.

Mohit and the team started with an observation about an everyday gesture: dragging an object. Design tools usually interpret that as an instruction about placement, but there’s much more intent in what a designer moves, where they move it and how they move it.

Placing an illustrated car into a parking space, for example, can involve separately adjusting its perspective, scale and style. The team asked whether the gesture itself could communicate more of that creative direction and help adapt the object to its surroundings, while keeping the result editable.

Yes. In our current prototype, a creativity slider lets the designer guide how subtle or expressive the adaptation should be, from preserving more of the original form to exploring a more dramatic transformation.
The goal is to combine the ease of a gesture with explicit creative control. The resulting vector artwork remains editable, so designers can continue refining it.

Two contrasting styles don’t necessarily need to become one. The key is understanding the creator’s intent: should the object match the scene, retain its own personality, or create a deliberate contrast?

Project Link Up explores combining the drag gesture and scene context with creative controls and prompt guidance. A designer could specify “match the scene’s illustration style” or “keep this character’s style, but adapt its perspective and lighting.”
The aim is to help designers steer the relationship between elements, while keeping the resulting vector artwork editable.

The philosophy is to make creative exploration more immediate. When combining two elements requires substantial adjustment before you can judge whether an idea works, that effort can interrupt the process of discovery.

Link Up explores how a familiar gesture could let designers try different relationships between objects, see what happens and develop the ideas they find interesting. Keeping the result editable as vector artwork matters: a promising combination becomes something the designer can continue shaping.

A strong example is manually reworking an asset to fit a new scene, particularly redrawing it from a different perspective. The team is exploring how that adaptation could happen as the designer places the object. That could reduce the preparation needed to evaluate a composition and give designers more time to refine the creative decisions that make it work.

A major direction in our research is helping tools understand creative content and the relationships within it. That understanding can make interactions more meaningful: moving an object into a scene could communicate an intention about perspective or composition, rather than simply a new position.

For experienced designers, the opportunity is to express their judgment more directly and retain precise control over the result. Link Up explores one part of that future. We want to learn what creators expect a gesture to mean and how tools can respond in ways that feel useful and predictable.
For more MAX news, check out Adobe's new Photoshop 2027 features.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: So, what are the best AI video generators, and how do they compare on price?
paragraphs: AI video generation has matured at an astonishing speed. One minute people were mocking attempts to generate footage of Will Smith eating spaghetti, the next we have tools capable of generating footage for everything from photorealistic commercials and animated explainers to social media ads and cinematic short films, all based on simple text prompts.

But choosing the best AI video generator for you isn't only a question of visual quality. The increasing number of models available have varying limitations and strengths and weaknesses in different areas. Pricing structures can also vary wildly, and subscription fees often represent only a fraction of the cost.

Many AI video generators operate on credit systems, charge extra for premium models, or limit video length and resolution in ways that can quickly inflate your spend. With that in mind, here we take a deeper dive into the five best AI video generators available today, which we've ranked according to overall value as well as their flexibility and practical usefulness for professional creatives.
Whichever model or models you choose to work with, you'll probably want one of the best laptops for video editing or the best desktop PCs for video editors.
Multiple models and a powerful ecosystem make this the best AI video generator overall
Integrated with Premiere Pro and Creative Cloud
Easier asset management than most competitors
Includes access to third-party models, including Google Veo, Kling and Runway.
Not always the highest visual quality available
Best value requires an existing Creative Cloud subscription

Adobe is already a powerhouse in filmmaking thanks to Premiere, which we rate as the best video editing software. As a result, Firefly more than just an AI video generator. Unlike many rivals that function as standalone tools, it integrates into Premiere and the wider Creative Cloud environment, making it significantly easier to incorporate AI-generated footage into existing professional workflows.

The most recent video-generation capabilities are particularly impressive. Prompt adherence is strong, footage tends to look polished and cinematic, and Adobe has invested heavily in making outputs commercially viable for professional users.

As announced at Adobe Max 2026, the native Firefly Video editor has been expanded to make it easier to combine clips with other elements such as images and sound effects, and projects created in Firefly Boards, Adobe's collaborative brainstorming space, can be carried straight into the video editor. There's also Adobe's AI agent, which makes using its software more intuitive and conversational.

The Adobe name also offers reassurance in terms of safety and reliability. The platform's unlikely to disappear or radically change from one day to the next, and output from the native Firefly Video Models is intended to be safer for commercial use since they were trained on licensed material rather than scaped copyrighted video.

On the other hand, if you do want to use other models, they're here in Firefly itself. Google Veo, Kling, Runway and Luma AI's Ray are all integrated and ready to use in Adobe's platform, so you get not only the top AI video generator on our list but access to the second, third and fourth too!

Pricing: Adobe's Firefly Standard plan costs $9.99 per month and includes 2,000 generative credits, enough for around twenty 5-second AI video clips at 1080p quality. Higher-tier plans increase those allowances. Adobe currently prices 1080p video generation at roughly 100 credits per second, meaning a single 5-second clip consumes around 500 credits.

You can also access Firefly video generation through a Creative Cloud Pro plan, which gives you access to Adobe's suite of apps, including Premiere and Photoshop. Just note that you may need to pay for additional generative credits depending on how much footage you're generating, and partner models have different credit costs.
Limited creative control compared to professional editing tools
Availability varies depending on subscription tier
Access typically comes through Google's AI subscription plans, with higher-end features reserved for more expensive tiers.

If pure visual quality is your priority, Google Veo has a strong claim to being the most impressive video model currently available. The platform is particularly good at realistic movement, lighting, camera behaviour and environmental detail.
Veo's ability to generate convincing cinematic scenes has made it popular among advertisers, content creators and filmmakers seeking premium-looking footage without a full production budget.

Pricing: Google offers Veo through consumer subscriptions and API access. For developers, Veo 3.1 costs roughly $0.40 per generated second, putting a typical 5-second clip at around $2.00 before retakes. That's easily the most expensive platform in this comparison, but it also delivers some of the highest-quality output available.

You can also access Veo through Google Gemini, Google AI Studio and through Adobe Firefly (see above). Through Gemini, there is a free tier offering just 3 video generations a day, at the time of writing, Google AI Pro costs $19.99 a month for 1,000 Flow credits, which translates to around 100 Lite videos or 10 high-quality Standard videos at 720p with a watermark. Google Ultra AI takes at $99.99 a month and upwards gives you 25,000 credits a month, enough to generate thousands of draft clips at 1080p.

Runway remains one of the most mature AI video platforms on the market. While some competitors may occasionally produce more realistic footage, Runway excels at putting creators in control. The platform includes advanced camera controls, editing features and creative tools that make it particularly appealing to professionals who want more than simple text-to-video generation.

The video editing features enable you to do things such as isolate a subject and remove the background, colour grading, adjusting the depth of field, making a slow motion version of your footage, and 'Inpainting', which means you can easily remove unwanted objects.

Pricing: Runway has several subscription tiers, ranging from entry-level plans through to professional and enterprise options. The credit-based system rewards efficient users but can become costly during experimentation. The Standard plan starts at $15 per month and includes 625 credits. According to Runway's published figures, that's enough for around 52 seconds of Gen-4.5 video generation. A creator producing multiple social videos every week will likely need the Pro plan at $35 per month or higher.
Interface can occasionally feel less intuitive
Quality isn't always as consistent as rivals
The Chinese platform Kling has become one of the biggest disruptors in AI video generation. It consistently produces impressive results while undercutting many western competitors on price.

Human movement, character animation and stylised content are particular strengths. For YouTubers, social creators and small businesses, Kling often represents the best balance between quality and affordability.

Pricing: Paid plans start at under $10 per month, and a 5-second 1080p clip generally consumes around 40 credits. That works out to roughly $0.40-$0.60 per clip depending on subscription tier, making Kling one of the most cost-effective premium AI video generators currently available and generally cheaper than Veo and Runway. However, as with most platforms, higher-quality generations consume credits faster.
Best for rapid experimentation and concept development
Lack of professional workflow integrations

Not every project needs blockbuster-quality visuals. Sometimes speed matters more than perfection, and that's where Hailuo shines. The platform is built around rapid iteration, allowing creators to test ideas quickly and cheaply. Agencies often use it during concept development before moving final production to more advanced systems.

Pricing: Hailuo is typically among the most affordable options available. Standard plans start between $8 and $15 per month depending on promotions and region. A typical 1080p generation consumes about 50 credits, placing the cost per clip around $0.50-$0.75.

The main trade-off is quality, and you might find yourself generating more clips to achieve a satisfactory result, which can offset the initial cost advantage. Additional editing and post-production work may also be required.

Before diving in to AI video generation, it's worth remembering that subscriptions don't always tell the whole story. A $10-per-month plan may sound inexpensive, but the number of usable clips you can generate could be surprisingly limited.
Making direct comparisons between AI video generators is difficult because some services charge per second of output, while others use credit systems that effectively works out as a cost per clip.

Pricing can also vary depending on which plan you choose and how much you use it. Heavy users are likely to have to pay extra for more credits, and plans are continually in flux. Providers have been making regular changes to their pricing as new models roll out and the competitive landscape changes. The prices being quoted today could easily change in a few weeks' time.

The challenge with any AI video generation is that creating a complete project often requires multiple generations. A single eight-second clip may be excellent, but producing several matching shots for a finished sequence can dramatically increase usage costs. You'll often need to generate dozens of variations before selecting a final clip, turning what appeared to be a modest monthly subscription into a much larger operational cost.
Users will also usually need separate editing software to assemble final productions.

For most creative professionals, we think Adobe Firefly currently represents the most balanced and versatile package while also offering reasonable value. While Google Veo may edge ahead on raw visual realism and Runway offers deeper creative controls, Firefly's integration with professional creative software makes it the most practical choice for real-world production environments, and Firefly does also provide access to Veo and Runway too.

That said, the right tool depends heavily on your needs. Consider Veo for cinematic quality, Runway for directorial control, Kling for affordability and Hailuo for rapid experimentation. Just don't judge any platform by its headline subscription price. In the AI video market, credits, render limits, premium models and editing requirements often matter far more than the monthly fee itself.

items.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
paragraphs: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.
A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.
The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

items.title: 5 wild Adobe Sneaks that creatives need to know about
paragraphs: At Adobe Max 2026 in Miami today, we got glimpses of where Adobe's creative software could go next with the traditional Adobe Sneaks reveals. Always a highlight of the annual event, the teasers reveal the tech and tools that could come to Adobe apps sometime in the future (and they do tend to arrive in some form).

Unsurprisingly, this year's Sneaks have a heavy focus on AI across the ten innovations. We saw demos of tools that could make AI image and video editing more precise and transform the workflows of people working in film, digital art, photography and design. Here are the highlights.

On the video and filmmaking front, Adobe's revealed what it's calling Project Scene Sweep. The AI-driven tool is being designed to understand characters, locations and scenes across a sequence, helping creators apply an edit consistently across cuts and camera angles.

It allows long-form, multi-shot videos to be edited from a single text prompt or edited frame, with the changes applied across each shot, cut, and camera angle. Example use cases cited include post-production fixes like removing a person or prop or swapping wardrobe without a reshoot.

The tool could also help for clearance issues, for example to replace an unlicensed logo or artwork in every shot where it appears, or for product placement after a shoot. Adobe suggests it could even be used to recast a new lead or location for a video or for testing variants for localisation.

Other projects in the works for video editing are Project Sound Bender, which would allow users to describe a sound and pull it out of a finished mix, then explore variations on an interactive canvas, and Project Live Set, which would allow filmmakers to change a subject or environment or redirect the camera as a scene continues.

For digital art and image editing, Project Deep Brush uses AI to understand an image’s shape, colour and lighting and separate images into physically decomposed layers. This would give artists a new level of control for painting and retouching, including the ability to control where paint lands and to make lighting-aware edits in photos.

Users would be able to add things like graffiti, signage, wraps, or branding to surfaces like walls, pillars, and vehicles, making the tool a potential game changer for product and environment mockups. For example, you could put a logo or texture on a curved or angled surface like a bottle, and the edit would follow the surface’s contours and lighting.
You'll be able to try this out for yourself on the new Adobe Labs Playground site.

Project Hands On is presented as a possible step from text-based editing towards a more fully graphical interface allowing greater control of AI-generated imagery. It analyses what’s in the image and then adds controls, such as control points that can be used to reshape details by simply dragging rather than rewriting a text prompt.
This could make editing AI-generated output more precise and intuitive, avoiding the trial-and-error nature of having to repeatedly rewrite prompts and regenerate an image.

Project Screen Test was perhaps the wildest idea teased at Adobe Sneaks. It would allow character designers to talk with their fictional creations to learn more about them and how they might behave in a given situation. Yes, seriously!

The tool would allow creators to develop a character’s look, voice and personality, and then have a natural language dialogue with said character in order to explore who they are and how they might respond in different scenes. The character would effectively audition for you.
The idea is that this conversation could turn character development in generative filmmaking and game development into a more intuitive, expressive part of the storytelling process.

Project Sight Span is tool that feels a lot more familiar. It transforms an image into an interactive, navigable world that creators can step inside and explore freely. That exploration could be used to frame shots beyond the original image, and render new images or camera-controlled videos, a little like what some artists are already doing with Gaussian splats. Adobe reckons this could be useful for things like set design and world building.

Another highlight of Adobe Sneaks 2026 was Project Link Up. With existing vector tools, dragging an object onto another only determines where it lands. Project Link Up turns that drag gesture into semantic fusion, combining an understanding of both objects with drag path, velocity, and creative controls to shape how they influence each other in real time, while keeping the result fully editable as vector artwork.

The idea is that artists and designers would be able to place 2D or vector assets into scenes with automatic perspective matching, reducing the need to redraw objects at new viewing angles. For typography, it would be possible to merge illustrated elements with letterforms while keeping the type editable for branding, logotypes, and packaging design.
For more news from Adobe Max, see what's new in Photoshop 2027.
